// ❌ wrong — groups and edits correctly, renders no group rows and no editor
import { GroupModule, EditModule } from '@elitegrid/core'

You do not have to remember this, because the grid tells you in development:

[EliteGrid] GroupModule is registered but its "groupRow" component is missing,
so its output will not render. Import GroupModule from your adapter package
(@elitegrid/react, @elitegrid/vue, @elitegrid/vanilla) rather than from
@elitegrid/core — the adapter's copy is the one that carries the component.

The short rule: everything comes from @elitegrid/vue. You should never need to import from @elitegrid/core directly.

Two modules with a quirk

InfiniteScrollModule is not in AllModules

Infinite scroll and pagination are mutually exclusive — one replaces pages with endless scrolling, the other provides the pages. AllModules contains PaginationModule, so if it also contained InfiniteScrollModule every grid built with AllModules would warn about the conflict and then disable one of them.

It is also the kind of feature that must never switch on by surprise: an upgrade that silently turned a paginated server-side grid into an endlessly scrolling one would be a bug, not a gift. So you name it explicitly, and you drop pagination when you do:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [SortModule, InfiniteScrollModule],
  columns,
  dataSource,
  infiniteScroll: { pageSize: 100 },
})

MenuModule carries no behaviour

Every other module registers a plugin. MenuModule registers nothing — it exists purely as a bundling key for the column menu and the context menu components. Its only job is to let you leave two fairly large UI trees out of your bundle.

That means a hand-picked list must name it explicitly to keep the menus, even if you have configured them:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [SortModule, MenuModule], // without MenuModule, no ⋮ and no right-click menu
  columns,
  data,
  columnMenu: { enabled: true },
})

If you configure a menu without registering the module, you get a warning rather than silence:

[EliteGrid] The column menu and context menu need MenuModule, which is not
registered, so the ⋮ button and the right-click menu will not render. Add
MenuModule to `modules` (it is already in AllModules), or set
`columnMenu: { enabled: false }` to silence this.

Writing your own module

If you are building a package on top of EliteGrid and want to ship your own plugin, defineModule is the supported entry point:

import { createGrid, defineModule, defineBundle } from '@elitegrid/vue'

const AuditModule = defineModule({
  id: 'audit-log',
  key: 'audit',
  order: 90,
  create: (ctx) => new AuditPlugin(ctx.options),
})

// Several of your own modules under one name
const MyGridBundle = defineBundle({
  id: 'my-company-grid',
  dependsOn: [SortModule, FilterModule, AuditModule],
})

const grid = createGrid<Row>({ modules: [MyGridBundle], columns, data })

Use withUI if your module also owns a Vue component that the renderer should pick up, the same way GroupModule supplies its group row.

One caveat if you care about bundle size in your own package: declare your bundles as object literals where you can. A call like defineBundle({ … }) at the top level of a file is something a bundler cannot prove is harmless, so it keeps the call — and keeping the call keeps everything you passed to it. This matters for library authors, not for application code.

Checklist

  • Want the old behaviour with no thought? modules: [AllModules].
  • A feature does nothing? Its module is not in your list.
  • A feature behaves but renders nothing? You imported it from @elitegrid/core instead of @elitegrid/vue.
  • Using the column or context menu with a hand-picked list? Add MenuModule.
  • Using infinite scroll? Name InfiniteScrollModule and drop PaginationModule.
  • Keyboard navigation and screen-reader support need no module and cannot be removed.

Next: Columns covers what you can do with a column definition.

chapters.title: Row Grouping & Aggregation
chapters.blurb: Sections, aggregates, grand totals, sticky headings
chapters.html:
Grouping collapses rows that share a value into expandable sections — all invoices for a customer, all employees in a department — and puts a summary on each section heading.

Two features that ship together, because grouping without totals is half a feature:

  • Grouping builds the sections.
  • Aggregation computes the number on each heading — a sum, an average, your own function.

Requires GroupModule. Grouping adds a pipeline stage and a store namespace, so it is a real module in the original sense. Without it, grouping is ignored entirely and no section headings render. See Modules.

The smallest grouped grid

import { createGrid, GroupModule, Grid } from '@elitegrid/vue'

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [GroupModule],
  columns,
  data: invoices,
  grouping: {
    model: ['customer'],
  },
})

model is the list of columns to group by, outermost first. Two entries means two levels:

grouping: {
  model: ['region', 'customer'], // every customer nested inside its region
}

You can pass the ColumnDef object instead of the field name. Both are type-checked and both follow a rename:

const regionColumn = { field: 'region', header: 'Region' }

grouping: { model: [regionColumn, 'customer'] }

An entry that matches no column warns by name in development rather than silently grouping by nothing.

The column you group by disappears

This is the first surprise, and it is deliberate. Grouping by Customer hides the Customer column, because the value is already in the section heading — showing it again puts the same string on every row of the section.

If you want it back:

grouping: {
  model: ['customer'],
  keepGroupedColumns: true,
}

Why this is the default: a grouped column left visible shows every row its own group's value twice — the group label above it, the same value again in the cell. Hiding it is the behaviour nearly everyone wants, so it is the default, with one flag to opt out.

Aggregation — the number on the heading

A column shows nothing on a group row unless you tell it what to compute. Set value.aggregate on the column:

const columns: ColumnDef<Invoice>[] = [
  { field: 'customer', header: 'Customer' },
  {
    field: 'amount',
    header: 'Amount',
    value: { aggregate: 'sum' },
  },
  {
    field: 'daysLate',
    header: 'Days Late',
    value: { aggregate: 'avg' },
  },
]

Seven built-in names: 'sum', 'avg', 'min', 'max', 'count', 'first', 'last'.

A column with no aggregate renders blank on a group row — never the first child's value. That is a safety decision. Showing the first row's amount on a heading is how a reader comes to believe a group of 12 invoices is worth $2,400.

Your own aggregate

Pass a function instead. It receives the extracted values and the typed rows, because most real aggregates need a sibling field:

{
  field: 'amount',
  header: 'Amount',
  value: {
    // a weighted average needs the weight column
    aggregate: (values, rows) => {
      const totalWeight = rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.weight, 0)
      if (totalWeight === 0) return 0
      return rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.amount * r.weight, 0) / totalWeight
    },
  },
}
// "how many in this group are overdue"
value: { aggregate: (values, rows) => rows.filter((r) => r.overdue).length }

A typo in a built-in name is a compile error, not a blank cell — the names are a union resolved by a switch, not a string looked up in a registry at runtime.

There is no aggregate formatter, on purpose. display.formatter receives a TData row, and a group row is not one. If you want control over how an aggregate is displayed, return a string from a custom aggregate — that is the supported path.

Aggregates are computed from the leaves at every level, never folded up from the level below. Folding is wrong for any non-associative function: an avg over unequal group sizes, or any custom median, comes out wrong.

A grand total over everything

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  grandTotal: 'bottom', // or 'top'
}

The grand total is a pinned row, so it stays visible while you scroll, and it re-totals whenever a filter changes. It works with an empty model too — a totals row on an ungrouped grid:

grouping: { model: [], grandTotal: 'top' }

Controlling the group key

By default a group's key is the column's display value — the same text search and tooltips read. So a column shown as $1,234 groups as $1,234, and a formatter that maps a status code to a label groups by the label, with nothing written.

Two cases the default gets wrong, and both warn in development:

A cellRenderer column — a rendered node has no text to group on.

A Date column — every distinct instant becomes its own group, which is never what you want. Bucket it:

{
  field: 'issuedAt',
  header: 'Issued',
  group: {
    valueGetter: (row) => String(row.issuedAt.getFullYear()),
  },
}

Ordering the sections

{
  field: 'priority',
  header: 'Priority',
  group: {
    comparator: (a, b) => RANK[a] - RANK[b], // 'high' before 'low'
  },
}

group.comparator orders the sections. sort.comparator orders the rows inside a section. They are independent, and the distinction matters:

  • Sorting the grid by a grouped column flips the section order.
  • Sorting by any other column reorders rows inside each section and leaves the section order alone.

The default section order is a numeric-aware locale compare, so Item 2 sorts before Item 10.

Blocking the menu affordance

{ field: 'notes', header: 'Notes', group: { enabled: false } }

That removes "Group by this column" from the column menu. Grouping it programmatically still works — this gates the affordance, not the capability.

How the sections look

One column, or the full width

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  displayType: 'singleColumn', // default
  groupColumn: { header: 'Region', width: 220, minWidth: 120 },
}

'singleColumn' prepends one synthetic column holding the chevron, the key and the count, indented by depth. 'fullWidth' spans the heading across every column and leaves your data columns alone.

What starts open

grouping: {
  model: ['region', 'customer'],
  expandedByDefault: 1, // top level only
}

false (the default) starts everything closed, true everything open, and a number opens to that depth.

Counts

grouping: { model: ['region'], showCounts: false } // drop the "(12)"

Sticky headings

As you scroll inside a section its heading pins under the column header, and the end of its own section pushes it out. On by default — a feature nobody enables is a feature nobody has, and it costs nothing on a grid with one group.

Nested headings stack: at depth 2 both levels stay pinned, outermost above.

grouping: { model: ['region'], stickyGroups: false } // turn it off

The chip bar

A bar above the column header naming what you are grouped by, outermost first. Drag a chip to reorder a level, × to remove one.

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  panel: 'whenGrouped', // default — appears only once something is grouped
}

true keeps it always visible, false never. The default is 'whenGrouped' because the bar takes no column dropped onto it — an empty one cannot teach you to group, so it should not occupy space pretending to. Creating a grouping is the column menu's "Group by this column".

Collapsed sections that still say something

A collapsed section is a summary, not a dead end. collapsedPreview puts something behind the heading's label:

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  collapsedPreview: 'share',
}

'share' paints a faint proportion bar — this section's rows against the filtered total. It costs zero horizontal space, and the eye ranks the sections before reading a single number.

Or render anything you like:

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  collapsedPreview: ({ leafRows, share }) =>
    h(AvatarStack, { users: leafRows.slice(0, 5), dimmed: share < 0.1 }),
}

leafRows is this section's filtered rows, and share is leafRows.length over the filtered total as a 0–1 number — handed to you so a custom preview paints the same proportion without re-deriving the denominator and getting it wrong.

Off by default.

Replacing the heading cell

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  cellRenderer: ({ group, label, toggle }) =>
    h('button', { class: 'yg-my-heading', onClick: toggle }, [
      `${group.expanded ? '▾' : '▸'} ${label} — ${group.count} rows`,
    ]),
}
params What it is
label e.g. "Acme Corp (12)" — already honours showCounts and the locale
toggle() Expand or collapse this section
group.path Ordered keys from the root: ['EMEA', 'Acme Corp']
group.key This level's key — the last element of path
group.level 0 for a top-level section; -1 for the grand total
group.count Descendant row count, after filtering
group.aggregates Aggregate values by column id
group.expanded Current state
group.leaves Every descendant row

Selection

A group's checkbox selects everything under it, and the heading shows a tri-state box (checked / unchecked / partial) that follows its children:

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [GroupModule, SelectionModule],
  columns,
  data: invoices,
  selection: { mode: 'multiple' },
  grouping: { model: ['customer'], selectsChildren: true }, // default
})

With selectsChildren: false the checkbox is hidden, not disabled. A group row is not in the row model, so it cannot be selected as a thing in its own right — with its children off the table the box would be inert, and an inert checkbox is worse than none. The slot stays reserved so no cell shifts out from under its header.

Pagination

grouping: {
  model: ['customer'],
  paginateBy: 'rows', // default
}
  • 'rows' pages what the user actually sees, so the scrollbar and the row count stay honest. A section may straddle a page boundary.
  • 'groups' pages whole top-level sections — "25 customers per page".

Filtering a grouped grid

Nothing to configure, but worth knowing: the grouping stage runs after filter and search. Sections are built only from rows that survived them, which means an empty section cannot exist, counts always mean surviving rows, and there is no stale parent left behind.

Export

By default a CSV contains your rows, not your section headings — a spreadsheet user re-groups with a pivot table, and a file with summary rows interleaved is not a dataset.

grouping: { model: ['region'], exportGroups: true } // include the headings

Two things that are handled for you, and are worth knowing because the obvious expectation is wrong:

  • The columns you grouped by are always in the file, even though grouping hides them on screen. Hiding is a display decision, and a CSV has no headings to carry the value instead — a grid grouped by Department used to export a file with no Department column, carrying its grouping in row order alone.
  • An export does not depend on which sections are expanded. Rows come out in display order but not display membership, so collapsing everything does not produce a file of headings and no rows.

Driving it from code

api.setGroupModel(['region', 'customer']) // group, outermost first
api.setGroupModel([])                     // ungroup
api.getGroupModel()                       // [] when nothing is grouped

api.setGroupExpanded(['EMEA', 'Acme Corp'], true)
api.expandAllGroups()
api.collapseAllGroups()

A path is a plain string array, so it survives JSON and a page reload — which is what lets grid state restore which sections were open.

Events

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [GroupModule],
  columns,
  data: invoices,
  grouping: { model: ['region'] },
  events: {
    onGroupModelChange: (model) => console.log('grouped by', model),
    onGroupExpand: (path, expanded) => console.log(path, expanded),
  },
})

Gotchas

  • A group row is not one of your rows. It is a tagged object in the same flat list. If you write a custom renderer that walks rows, narrow with isGroupRow(row) before assuming you have a TData. Your own rows are untouched and still passed by reference.
  • A column with no value.aggregate is blank on a heading. That is intentional; see above.
  • Date and cellRenderer columns need group.valueGetter. Both warn in development.
  • keepGroupedColumns is false by default — the column you grouped by vanishes until you ask for it back.
  • exportGroups is false by default — headings are not in your CSV unless you ask.
  • GroupModule must come from @elitegrid/vue, not @elitegrid/core. Core's copy groups correctly and renders no headings at all. It warns if you get this wrong.

Next: Row Features covers pinned rows, row numbers, drag-to-reorder and expandable detail rows.

chapters.title: Row Features
chapters.blurb: Pinned rows, row numbers, auto-height, detail rows, drag to reorder
chapters.html:
Five things you can do to a row that are not sorting, filtering or editing it:

Feature What it does Module
Pinned rows Freeze rows above or below the scrolling body none
Row numbers An ordinal strip down the left edge none
Auto-height Rows that grow to fit their content none
Detail rows A row expands to reveal a panel none
Drag to reorder Drag a row somewhere else in the list none

None of them needs a module. They ride on ViewportPlugin, which is mandatory, so they all work on a grid built with modules: [].

Pinned top and bottom rows

Rows frozen above or below the scrolling body:

const grid = createGrid<Employee>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data: employees,
  pinnedRows: {
    top: [{ id: 'hdr', name: 'Engineering', salary: 0 }],
    bottom: [summaryRow],
  },
})

They are the same TData shape as a body row, which means every column option you already wrote — display.formatter, display.cellRenderer, display.tooltip — works on them unchanged.

A pinned row is presentation, not data. It is not in the row model, so it is never filtered, sorted, paginated, selected, focused, edited, exported or copied, and api.getData() does not include it. That is one rule covering every question you might have about how pinned rows interact with anything else: they don't.

Change them at runtime:

api.setPinnedRows('bottom', [newSummary])
api.setPinnedRows('top', []) // clear

For a totals row, do not build one here. Set grouping.grandTotal and let value.aggregate compute it — that row is pinned too, and it re-totals on every filter. See Row Grouping.

Row numbers

An automatic ordinal strip down the left edge, left of the selection checkbox:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({ modules: [], columns, data, rowNumbers: true })

true means "every default". There is no rowNumbers.enabled — the option's presence is the enable.

rowNumbers: {
  count: 'result', // default
  start: 1,        // default; 0 gives 0-based numbering
  width: 56,       // default — five digits at the default font
  header: '#',     // default comes from the locale
}

Which ordinal

This is the part worth choosing deliberately:

count Meaning
'result' (default) Position in the filtered + sorted result, running continuously across pages — page 3 of 20 starts at 41
'page' Restarts at 1 on every page
'source' Position in the original data array — immune to filter, search, sort and pagination

Naming these three is the feature: without them, every developer who cares about the difference ends up writing the same function.

Custom text

rowNumbers: {
  format: ({ row, index }) => `${row.department}-${index}`,
}

params.row is your own TData, not an any you have to cast.

It is not a column. The strip is never in columns.definitions, so it is never sorted, filtered, resized, pinned, reordered, hidden, focused, exported, or saved into a grid state view. If you need any of those, you want a real column with a valueGetter, not this.

Rows that size themselves

Every row is appearance.rowHeight (default 40) until something asks for more. Set display.wrap on a column and that column's text wraps, the row grows to fit, and rowHeight becomes the minimum rather than the fixed height:

const columns: ColumnDef<Ticket>[] = [
  { field: 'title', header: 'Title' },
  { field: 'description', header: 'Description', display: { wrap: true } },
]

Capping it

appearance: {
  rowHeight: 40,
  maxRowHeight: 160,
}

Uncapped is the default on purpose: a cap silently clips content, which is worse than one tall row. Instead, development mode warns once the first time a row exceeds 10× rowHeight and points you here.

Per-row control

appearance: {
  getRowHeight: (params) => {
    if (params.kind === 'group') return 32
    return params.row.pinned ? 72 : undefined // undefined = let the grid decide
  },
}

params is a discriminated union — { kind: 'row', row } or { kind: 'group', group } — so the group-row case is a branch the compiler makes you handle.

Called for every row of the display list, so keep it synchronous and cheap.

From code

api.setRowHeight('row-42', 120)
api.setRowHeight('row-42', null) // back to automatic
api.resetRowHeights()

One call — there is no separate refresh to remember afterwards.

Expandable detail rows

A row expands to reveal a panel underneath it. Supplying renderer is what turns the feature on — there is no rowDetail.enabled:

const grid = createGrid<Order>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data: orders,
  rowDetail: {
    renderer: ({ row }) =>
      h('div', { class: 'p-4' }, [
        h('h4', null, row.customer),
        h(LineItems, { items: row.items }),
      ]),
  },
})

params.row is your own TData, and the return type is Vue's VNode — neither of them is any.

rowDetail: {
  renderer: ({ row }) => h(OrderDetail, { order: row }),

  // Which rows can expand. Default: all of them.
  isExpandable: (row) => row.items.length > 0,

  // Rows open on first render, by row id.
  defaultExpanded: ['order-1'],

  // At most one row open at a time. Opening a second closes the first.
  single: true,

  // Where the chevron goes. Default 'first-column'.
  toggle: 'first-column',

  // Assumed panel height until it has been measured. Default 200.
  estimatedHeight: 240,
}

estimatedHeight is an estimate, not a setting

The grid needs some number to lay out with before your panel exists — it is your component, so there is no string to measure. Once the panel paints, the auto-height pass measures it and corrects the row. Setting this near the real height means the grid never visibly corrects; leaving it means one small correction the first time a row opens.

One number, and it self-corrects — there is no second "measure instead" switch to find.

Driving it from code

api.expandRow('order-1')
api.collapseRow('order-1')
api.toggleRowExpanded('order-1')
api.isRowExpanded('order-1')
api.getExpandedRows()
api.expandAllRows()
api.collapseAllRows()

It is toggleRowExpanded, not toggleRow. toggleRow is taken — it toggles row selection. Two different things called "toggling a row" is exactly the ambiguity the longer name buys out.

All of these are synchronous and take the same row id string as setRowHeight and flashCells. The three opening calls warn in development if the feature is off or the row is not expandable; the two closing calls stay silent, because asking to close something already closed got the outcome it asked for.

expandAllRows() warns past about 1,000 rows rather than refusing — on a filtered set of 20 it is reasonable, on 100k it almost certainly is not, and the call cannot tell them apart.

Your own chevron

rowDetail: {
  renderer: ({ row }) => h(OrderDetail, { order: row }),
  toggle: 'none',
}

// then, in a column:
{
  field: 'customer',
  header: 'Customer',
  display: {
    cellRenderer: ({ row }) =>
      h('button', { onClick: () => api.toggleRowExpanded(String(row.id)) }, [
        row.customer,
      ]),
  },
}

toggle: 'none' is the escape hatch, not the default — configuring it and then never calling toggleRowExpanded() warns in development.

Drag to reorder

const grid = createGrid<Task>({ modules: [], columns, data, rowDrag: true })

That is the whole configuration for the common case.

rowDrag: {
  // Where the grip lives. Default 'first-column'.
  //   'first-column'       inside the first visible column's cells
  //   'row'                the whole row is draggable
  //   { column: 'name' }   a specific column
  handle: 'first-column',

  isDraggable: (row) => !row.locked,
  canDrop: ({ row, target }) => target.status === row.status,
  whenSorted: 'disable', // or 'clear-sort'
  dragPreview: ({ row }) => h(Pill, null, [row.title]), // null for none
}

It works filtered, sorted and paged

Worth stating plainly, because the competing implementation does not: a drop is resolved against the neighbour you dropped on, not against a display index. So dragging works on a filtered list and across pages.

When a sort is active

The one case with no good answer, so it is a choice you make:

  • 'disable' (default) — the handle renders disabled, with a localized tooltip saying why.
  • 'clear-sort' — freezes the visible order into the data and drops the sort. This is the only reading under which the gesture does what it looked like it did.

A development warning names this option the first time it bites.

The drag preview

What follows the pointer. The default is a pill showing the row's first visible cell — on touch, the row under the finger is the row you cannot see. Return null for no preview.

From code

api.moveRow('task-3', 0)                     // to the top
api.moveRows(['task-3', 'task-9'], 5)

Reacting to a reorder

events: {
  onRowOrderChanged: ({ source }) => {
    // `source` says whether this was a drag or an api.moveRow() call
    persistOrder(api.getData())
  },
}

Gotchas

  • Pinned rows are invisible to everything else — no filter, sort, selection, export or getData(). If you need a row to participate, it belongs in data.
  • rowNumbers is a strip, not a column. Nothing that works on columns works on it.
  • maxRowHeight is uncapped by default, and a cap clips. Prefer the warning.
  • getRowHeight must handle the 'group' branch — the compiler will tell you.
  • rowDetail.renderer is the enable. No renderer, no feature, and every expansion API call is a no-op.
  • toggleRowExpanded ≠ toggleRow. The short name is selection.
  • A drag under an active sort does nothing by default. Set whenSorted: 'clear-sort' if the gesture should win.

Next: 09 · Appearance & Theming

chapters.title: Menus & Clipboard
chapters.blurb: The column menu, right-click menu, and copy to clipboard
chapters.html:
Three features that share a theme — getting data and commands out of the grid without writing a toolbar:

  • The column menu — the ⋮ button in a column header.
  • The context menu — right-click in the body.
  • Clipboard copy — Ctrl/Cmd+C, and the API behind it.

The two menus need MenuModule, which carries no behaviour of its own — it exists purely so the two menu component trees can be left out of a bundle that does not want them. It is in AllModules. Clipboard copy needs no module at all.

Configure a menu without registering MenuModule and you get a development warning rather than silence.

The column menu

On by default wherever MenuModule is registered:

import { createGrid, AllModules, Grid } from '@elitegrid/vue'

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  columnMenu: {
    enabled: true,      // default
    showOnHover: false, // default — the ⋮ is always visible
    showColumnChooser: true, // default
  },
})
Option Default Meaning
enabled true Show the ⋮ button at all
showOnHover false Reveal the button only while the header is hovered
icon ⋮ Replace the glyph with your own node
showColumnChooser true The inline checkbox list of every column
items — Rewrite the item list

Keyboard focus and an open menu reveal the button regardless of showOnHover, so it is never unreachable.

Turning showColumnChooser off while the menu still offers "Hide column" warns in development — a hidden column would then have no route back.

What is in it

Item id What it does
sortAsc / sortDesc / clearSort Sorting
filter Opens this column's filter
groupBy / ungroup Row grouping
pinLeft / pinRight / unpin Column pinning
autoSizeThis / autoSizeAll Column auto-size
hide Hide this column
columns The inline column chooser

Each item appears only when the module behind it is registered — no SortModule, no sort items.

Rewriting the items

columnMenu: {
  items: ({ column, columnId, defaultItems, api }) => [
    ...defaultItems.filter((i) => i.id !== 'hide'),
    {
      id: 'copy-column',
      label: `Copy all of ${column.header}`,
      separator: true,
      action: () => api.copyToClipboard({ columns: [columnId], scope: 'filtered' }),
    },
  ],
}

defaultItems holds real objects with live actions, so both of these work:

defaultItems.filter((i) => i.id !== 'hide')        // drop one
defaultItems.map((i) => i.id === 'sortAsc' ? { ...i, label: 'A→Z' } : i)  // rename one

An item takes:

Field Meaning
id A built-in id, or any string for your own
label The text
icon Your own node
disabled Greyed out, with aria-disabled
checked Draws a check and makes it a radio row. undefined ≠ false — undefined means "no checked state"
separator Draw a rule above this item
action(params) What it does

separator lives on the item rather than being its own array entry, so filtering defaultItems can never strand a separator at the top or bottom of the menu.

Per-column tweaks

{
  field: 'notes',
  header: 'Notes',
  menu: {
    enabled: true,
    items: ({ defaultItems }) => defaultItems.filter((i) => i.id !== 'groupBy'),
  },
}

The grid-level columnMenu.items runs first, and the per-column menu.items runs on its output — so a grid-wide addition and a per-column tweak compose instead of one silently replacing the other.

The context menu

Right-click in the body:

contextMenu: {
  enabled: true,                // default — governs the BODY
  openColumnMenuOnHeader: true, // default
}
Item id Needs
copy / copyWithHeaders nothing
export / exportSelection ExportModule
expandAll / collapseAll GroupModule or rowDetail
autoSizeAll nothing
moveToTop / moveToBottom rowDrag

copy and autoSizeAll are ungated, so a grid built with modules: [] still gets a working right-click menu.

The browser's menu

When enabled is false the browser's own menu appears, because the grid suppresses it only when it shows its own. That one rule is the whole of the configuration.

Returning [] from items does the same thing, per target:

contextMenu: {
  items: ({ target, defaultItems }) =>
    target.kind === 'blank' ? [] : defaultItems, // browser menu outside cells
}

Right-clicking a header

openColumnMenuOnHeader (default true) opens that column's ⋮ menu at the pointer instead of the context menu. It is independent of enabled, which governs the body — a grid can legitimately want one and not the other.

The target

contextMenu: {
  items: ({ target, defaultItems, api }) => {
    if (target.kind === 'blank') return defaultItems
    return [
      ...defaultItems,
      {
        id: 'open',
        label: `Open ${target.row.customer}`,
        separator: true,
        action: () => router.push(`/invoices/${target.rowId}`),
      },
    ]
  },
}

target.kind is 'cell' or 'blank'. On a cell you get row (a real TData, by reference, never a group row), rowId, columnId and column.

Per-column context items

{
  field: 'secret',
  header: 'Secret',
  menu: {
    contextItems: () => [], // browser's menu over this column
  },
}

Named contextItems rather than a second items because both live in one group.

Opening it yourself

api.showContextMenu({ x: event.clientX, y: event.clientY })

Viewport coordinates — the same numbers a MouseEvent carries. That is the whole binding for a long-press on touch, a toolbar button or a custom keybinding.

This is deliberately not gated on contextMenu.enabled: a developer who turned the built-in right-click off and bound their own gesture is exactly the caller this method has. enabled governs the gesture the grid owns, not the feature.

Clipboard copy

Ctrl/Cmd+C copies the selection, or the focused cell if nothing is selected. On by default — copying what you selected is baseline behaviour, not a feature you opt into.

clipboard: {
  enabled: true,          // default — governs the SHORTCUT only
  includeHeaders: false,  // default
  delimiter: '\t',        // default
}

The default delimiter is a tab, because Excel, Sheets and Numbers all parse tab-separated paste into cells. A comma produces a single column in all three.

includeHeaders is off because a one-cell copy with a header line above it is wrong far more often than it is right — and a single focused cell never gets one regardless of the setting.

enabled: false disables the shortcut, not the feature. api.copyToClipboard() keeps working, because an API call is an explicit request rather than an affordance the grid offered.

From code

const result = await api.copyToClipboard({
  scope: 'selected',       // 'auto' | 'focused' | 'all' | 'filtered' | 'page' | 'selected'
  includeHeaders: true,
  columns: ['name', 'amount'],
  delimiter: ',',
})

if (!result.ok) {
  toast(result.reason === 'denied' ? 'Clipboard blocked' : 'Nothing to copy')
}

It returns a result rather than void:

Field Meaning
ok false when nothing was copied — the clipboard is left untouched, never overwritten with an empty string
text Exactly what was written, header row included
rowCount Rows written, excluding the header. A one-cell copy is 1 × 1
columnCount Columns written
reason Only when ok is false
reason Cause
'empty' Nothing selected, no focused cell, or no columns resolved
'unavailable' No clipboard host — server-side rendering, or a call before mount
'denied' The browser blocked it: non-secure context, denied permission, or no user gesture

Every copy method returns a result, so a clipboard write that the browser refuses is something you can see and handle rather than a silent no-op.

Gotchas

  • Both menus need MenuModule. It is in AllModules; a hand-picked list must name it. Configuring a menu without it warns.
  • columnMenu.items runs before column.menu.items, and the per-column one receives the output of the grid-level one.
  • checked: undefined is not checked: false. Undefined means the item has no checked state at all and stays a plain menuitem.
  • A menu item's separator draws a rule above itself, so filtering items never strands one.
  • clipboard.enabled: false still leaves api.copyToClipboard() working.
  • copyToClipboard can fail for reasons that are not your bug — a non-secure context or a missing user gesture. Check result.ok.
  • Floating menus portal to document.body, so they carry the grid's theme classes with them. If you are building your own floating surface, do the same or it will render light on a dark grid.

Next: Live & Streaming Data.

chapters.title: Live & Streaming Data
chapters.blurb: Transactions, infinite scroll, cell flash
chapters.html:
Three features for a grid whose data arrives while the user is looking at it:

  • Transactions — many row changes in one repaint.
  • Infinite scroll — fetch the next page as the user nears the bottom.
  • Cell flash — briefly highlight what just changed.

Transactions

Calling addRow() 500 times runs the whole pipeline 500 times. A transaction is many mutations in one pipeline pass and one repaint:

const result = api.applyTransaction({
  add: [newOrder],
  update: [{ id: 7, price: 19.99 }],
  remove: ['order-3', 'order-4'],
})

Needs no module and no configuration.

Field Takes
add Rows to insert
addIndex Where to insert — an index after removals are applied. Omit to append
update Partial<TData> changes, merged onto the existing row
remove Row ids — an array or a Set

update merges, it does not replace

A delta feed sends { id, price } and the row's other fields survive:

// row was { id: 7, name: 'Widget', price: 10, stock: 4 }
api.applyTransaction({ update: [{ id: 7, price: 12 }] })
// row is now { id: 7, name: 'Widget', price: 12, stock: 4 }

Each entry must carry enough for the configured rowId to resolve it — the id field for rowId: 'field', or every field the function reads for rowId: (row) => …. Entries that cannot be resolved are skipped and reported, not guessed at.

A partial update is a patch, not a replacement — you send the fields that changed, not the whole row.

remove takes ids

api.applyTransaction({ remove: api.getSelectedIds() })

That is the single most likely call anyone writes, so a Set is accepted as well as an array. A bare string is deliberately not accepted — remove: 'row-1' would otherwise iterate into deleting rows 'r', 'o', 'w'…

The result tells you what happened

const result = api.applyTransaction({ update: feed })

if (result.skipped.length > 0) {
  console.warn('feed ids have drifted', result.skipped)
}
Field Meaning
added Rows actually inserted, in insertion order
updated Rows after the merge — not the partials you passed
removed Rows as they were immediately before deletion
skipped Ops that were dropped, and why. Empty on a clean transaction
applied true when at least one row changed

applied is not the same as skipped.length === 0 — a transaction can add two rows and skip a third.

A skip carries { op, id?, reason, index }, where reason is one of:

reason Cause
'duplicate-id' add: a row with this id is already in the grid
'unknown-id' update / remove: no row with this id
'unresolvable-id' update: the configured rowId could not derive an id from the partial
'invalid-entry' remove: not a string. add / update: not an object

An update for an unknown id is reported rather than dropped — a feed whose ids have drifted should not go unnoticed for a week.

A busy feed

If messages arrive faster than you want to repaint, coalesce them:

const grid = createGrid<Tick>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data,
  transactions: { waitMs: 50 }, // default
})

socket.on('tick', (t) => {
  api.applyTransactionAsync({ update: [t] })
})

applyTransactionAsync returns a promise resolving to the same TransactionResult, and never rejects.

The timer is one per window, not per call: message 500 does not reset the clock message 1 started, so a busy feed still flushes every waitMs instead of being starved indefinitely.

api.flushTransactions() // apply everything queued, now

You only need flushTransactions() when your own code must see the rows — before a screenshot, a print, or a route change. A synchronous applyTransaction() flushes the queue first on its own.

Before mount and during server-side rendering there is no timer, so an async transaction applies immediately and resolves with the same result. Nothing is lost but the coalescing.

The event

events: {
  onTransaction: (result) => console.log(result.added.length, 'added'),
}

Fires once per applied applyTransaction(), after the pipeline settles — so api.getDisplayedRows() inside it is fresh. A transaction that changed nothing does not fire it.

onRowAdd / onRowUpdate / onRowDelete still fire per row for the same transaction, deliberately: suppressing them would mean a developer who wired onRowDelete sees nothing when a transaction deletes.

Infinite scroll

"Load 100 rows, then fetch the next 100 as the user nears the bottom" — no pagination bar.

import { createGrid, InfiniteScrollModule, Grid } from '@elitegrid/vue'

const dataSource = {
  async getRows({ page, pageSize, sortModel, filterModel, search }) {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/orders?page=${page}&size=${pageSize}`)
    const { rows, total } = await res.json()
    return { rows, totalCount: total }
  },
}

const grid = createGrid<Order>({
  modules: [InfiniteScrollModule],
  columns,
  dataSource,
  infiniteScroll: {
    threshold: 20, // default — rows of lead time before the next fetch
    pageSize: 100, // defaults to pagination.pageSize, then to 100
  },
})

Two requirements:

  • dataSource, not data.
  • InfiniteScrollModule, named explicitly. It is deliberately not in AllModules, because it is mutually exclusive with PaginationModule — and because an upgrade that silently turned a server-paginated grid into an endlessly scrolling one would be a bug, not a gift.

pageSize is deliberately the same key the grid already has rather than a second "block size" concept — a developer who set pagination.pageSize: 100 and then switched to infinite scroll should not have to discover a new name for the number they already chose.

Two keys, and no second datasource interface. There is no cache to evict, no overflow to size and no concurrency to cap, because the loaded region is contiguous rather than sparse.

Driving and observing it

await api.loadMore()   // fetch the next page now
api.hasMoreRows()      // false once totalCount is reached
events: {
  onLoadMore: ({ page, loadedCount, totalCount }) =>
    console.log(`${loadedCount} / ${totalCount}`),

  onLoadMoreError: ({ error, page }) => {
    toast(`Page ${page} failed`)
  },
}

When a fetch fails

The rows already loaded stay on screen, and api.loadMore() is the retry:

events: {
  onLoadMoreError: ({ error }) => {
    showRetryBanner(() => api.loadMore())
  },
}

The failure path takes the error, keeps the block retryable, and says so in the UI — a page that failed to load is not a page that is permanently blank.

Filtering and sorting

sortModel, filterModel and search are all handed to getRows so a server-side source can honour them. A change to any of the three discards the loaded pages and refetches from page 1, because rows 0–299 sorted here and rows 300+ ordered by the server would not agree.

Honouring them server-side is about which rows you get, not about who orders them. The grid still sorts the rows it holds; there is no mode that defers ordering to the data source. A source that ignores sortModel returns later pages from an unsorted set, which reads as correct within a page and wrong across pages.

Cell flash

Briefly highlight a cell whose value changed:

const grid = createGrid<Tick>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data,
  appearance: {
    flash: { enabled: true, duration: 600, onEdit: false },
  },
})

flash: true is exactly flash: { enabled: true }.

Option Default Meaning
enabled false Off by default
duration 600 ms, covering rise and fall
onEdit false Flash the cell the user just finished editing

Off by default because a grid that is not live-updating should not flash when the developer calls updateRow() from a form save.

onEdit is off because the user knows what they typed — a flash is for changes arriving from somewhere else.

One duration for the whole flash, rather than separate fade and hold halves nobody has an opinion about.

Per column

const columns: ColumnDef<Tick>[] = [
  { field: 'symbol', header: 'Symbol' },
  { field: 'price', header: 'Price', display: { flash: 'up-down' } },
  { field: 'updatedAt', header: 'Updated', display: { flash: false } },
]
display.flash Behaviour
unset Inherit appearance.flash.enabled
true Flash in the neutral highlight colour
'up-down' Green when the value rose, red when it fell
false Never flash this column

'up-down' on a non-numeric column falls back to the neutral flash and warns once for that column.

The usual shape is flash: true grid-wide with flash: false on a "Last Updated" column, which changes on every update and says nothing by flashing.

It cannot false-positive

The trigger is a data event. Filtering, sorting, searching, paging and scrolling never emit it, so none of them can flash a cell that did not change.

The trigger is a real value change, not a re-render — so filtering or scrolling never lights a cell up, and there is no option needed to undo that.

Flashing on demand

api.flashCells([
  { rowId: 'row-1', columnId: 'price' },
  { rowId: 'row-9' }, // the whole row
])

A list of cells, not a cross product. Asking for A1 and B2 lights up exactly those two.

The argument is a list of individual cells, not a row set crossed with a column set — so A1 and B2 flash without lighting up A2 and B1, which is the scattered shape a live feed actually produces. Rows are named by id string here, as they are everywhere else in the API.

Cells that are not currently rendered are still registered, and flash if they scroll into view before the window expires.

Gotchas

  • update merges; it does not replace. Send only what changed.
  • remove takes ids, not rows. A Set works.
  • Check result.skipped on anything fed from outside your app — a drifted id is otherwise invisible.
  • applied ≠ skipped.length === 0.
  • Infinite scroll needs dataSource, not data, and InfiniteScrollModule is not in AllModules.
  • Infinite scroll and pagination are mutually exclusive. Registering both warns and disables one.
  • Flash is off by default, and a failed fetch leaves loaded rows on screen rather than blanking them.

Next: 11 · Events

toc.text: update merges, it does not replace
The result tells you what happened

chapters.title: Localization & State
chapters.blurb: Translating every string; saving and restoring a view
chapters.html:
Two features that tax every other one, so they are worth setting up early:

  • Localization — every string the grid renders, overridable.
  • Grid state — saved views: column layout, sort, filters, search, grouping, pagination, selection, scroll.

Neither needs a module.

Localization

Every string the grid renders has a key, and you override the ones you care about:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  locale: {
    filterApply: 'Anwenden',
    filterClear: 'Löschen',
    filterOpContains: 'enthält',
  },
})

Partial by design. Anything you leave out stays English, so overriding three strings for tone is as legitimate as translating all 250.

Parameterised strings are functions

Not strings with placeholder tokens — which is what lets a translation reorder or pluralise them:

locale: {
  paginationPage: (page) => `Seite ${page}`,
  paginationRowCount: (from, to, total) => `${from}–${to} von ${total}`,
  groupCount: (count) => `${count} ${count === 1 ? 'Eintrag' : 'Einträge'}`,
}

A token-based string like 'Page {page} of {total}' cannot express a plural rule or a different word order. A function can.

Finding the keys

Keys are grouped by the surface they belong to, so autocomplete is useful:

Prefix Covers
filterOp* Filter operators — contains, between, before…
filter* The filter popover's own chrome
floatingFilter* The floating filter row
setFilter* The set filter's summary and list
pagination* The pagination bar
group* Group headings, counts, the chip bar, menu items

The full list with its English defaults is DEFAULT_LOCALE in the package source.

Catching what you missed

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  locale: myGermanLocale,
  localeStrict: true, // dev-only
})

Warns once, listing every key still rendering English. Opt-in rather than on by default, because a partial override is a legitimate choice rather than a mistake.

The grid's own label

accessibility: {
  gridLabel: 'Rechnungen', // overrides locale.gridLabel for this grid
}

accessibility.gridLabel predates locale and still wins for this one string — the narrow option beats the broad one.

Turning announcements down

accessibility: {
  announceFocus: true,      // default
  announceSort: true,       // default
  announceFilter: true,     // default
  announceSelection: true,  // default
  announceEdit: true,       // default
  announcePage: true,       // default
  announceRowsLoaded: true, // default — "200 of 12,480 rows loaded"
}

All on by default. See Accessibility.

Grid state

Everything the user arranged, in one serialisable object:

const saved = api.getState()
localStorage.setItem('myGrid', JSON.stringify(saved))
const report = api.setState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('myGrid')!))

Let the grid persist it for you

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  state: {
    key: 'invoices-grid', // persist here, restore on mount
    debounce: 200,        // default
  },
})

That is the whole setup — no serialiser, no debounce, no version check to write.

debounce defaults to 200ms because scroll alone fires per frame, and an undebounced write would be a synchronous serialise on the scroll path.

What a state holds

Slice Contents
columns Width, order, visibility, pinning — and which column groups are folded
sort The sort model
filters The filter model
search The quick-filter text
grouping { model, expanded } — which columns are grouped and which sections are open
pagination { page, pageSize }
selection { ids }
rowDetail { expanded } — row ids whose detail panel is open
scroll { top, left }

A slice is absent only when the module that owns it is not registered.

Group expansion survives a reload, because a group is addressed by its key path — plain strings that JSON handles with no custom serialiser, and nothing that points at an internal row object.

Choosing what to persist

state: {
  key: 'invoices-grid',
  include: ['columns', 'sort', 'filters'], // not selection or scroll
}

Default is every slice the grid produces.

Restoring a subset

api.setState(saved, { only: ['columns'] }) // layout back, filters untouched

A restore tells you what happened

const report = api.setState(saved)

if (report.skipped.length > 0) {
  console.warn('partial restore', report.skipped)
}
Field Meaning
applied Slices that were restored
skipped { slice, reason, detail? } for each one that was not
reason Cause
'absent-module' The module that owns the slice is not registered
'not-in-state' The saved object has no such slice
'excluded' You passed only and this slice was not in it
'schema-mismatch' The saved state is from an incompatible version

It returns a report rather than void, which is what makes a partial restore visible — otherwise a saved view comes back "mostly" and nobody notices the filters are missing until a user does. expect(report.skipped).toEqual([]) is a test anyone can write.

initial vs key

state: {
  initial: savedFromMyServer, // restore this object once
}

initial is applied once, after the first data settle — not at construction. With an async dataSource there are no rows yet when the grid is built, so a restored selection would select nothing and a restored scroll offset would exceed a zero-height canvas.

Pipeline inputs — columns, sort, filters, search, page size — still apply immediately.

key and initial are independent: key persists to storage and restores from it, initial restores an object you supply. Use initial when the state comes from your own server rather than the browser.

Reacting to changes

events: {
  onStateChange: (state) => saveToServer(state),
}

Already debounced by state.debounce, so it is safe to persist directly from here. It fires whether or not state.key is set.

Functions do not serialise

A comparator or customFilter declared on the column is re-attached on restore, so a column with a custom sort keeps it.

One passed imperatively — to setSortModel() or setColumnFilter() — is dropped, with a development warning. If you want a custom comparator to survive a saved view, declare it on the column.

Gotchas

  • locale is partial. Untranslated keys stay English silently; localeStrict: true in development is how you find them.
  • Parameterised locale entries are functions, not templates with tokens.
  • accessibility.gridLabel beats locale.gridLabel.
  • state.initial applies after the first data settle, not at construction — so a selection restore works with an async source.
  • Check report.skipped. A half-restored view is otherwise invisible.
  • Declare comparators on the column, not imperatively, if they must survive a restore.
  • A saved rowDetail is filtered against the rows that came back — a saved view of a deleted row does not reopen a panel for it.

Next: 13 · Accessibility
