chapters.title: Full Working Example
chapters.blurb: Everything combined in one file
chapters.html:
This chapter ties every feature together into one realistic, copy-pasteable page: an Employee grid with sorting, filtering, pagination, multiple selection, inline editing with validation, value formatting, CSV export, a custom toolbar driven by the Grid API, and event logging.

The same code lives as a runnable file in examples/employee-grid.html.

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/node_modules/@elitegrid/vanilla/dist/styles.css" />
    <style>
      body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
      .toolbar { display: flex; gap: 8px; align-items: center; padding: 24px 24px 12px; }
      .grid-wrap { height: 520px; margin: 0 24px 24px; border: 1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius: 8px; }
      .salary-high { color: #16a34a; font-weight: 600; }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div class="toolbar">
      <strong id="selection-count">0 selected</strong>
      <button id="select-all">Select all</button>
      <button id="clear-selection">Clear</button>
      <button id="export-selected" disabled>Export selected</button>
      <button id="delete-selected" disabled>Delete selected</button>
      <button id="export-all">Export all (filtered)</button>
      <button id="clear-filters">Clear filters</button>
    </div>
    <div id="grid-container" class="grid-wrap"></div>

    <script type="module">
      import { createGrid, AllModules, mount, buildGridAPI } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

      // ── 1. The data shape ────────────────────────────────────────────────
      // interface Employee {
      //   id: number
      //   name: string
      //   department: string
      //   salary: number
      //   active: boolean
      //   joinDate: string // ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD'
      // }

      const DEPARTMENTS = ['Engineering', 'Design', 'Marketing', 'HR', 'Finance']

      const employees = Array.from({ length: 200 }, (_, i) => ({
        id: i + 1,
        name: `Employee ${i + 1}`,
        department: DEPARTMENTS[i % DEPARTMENTS.length],
        salary: 50_000 + (i % 50) * 1_000,
        active: i % 3 !== 0,
        joinDate: new Date(2015, i % 12, (i % 28) + 1).toISOString().split('T')[0],
      }))

      // ── 2. Create the grid ─────────────────────────────────────────────
      const grid = createGrid({
        modules: [AllModules],
        // unique ID field — `id` is the default, shown here for clarity
        rowId: 'id',

        columns: [
          {
            field: 'name',
            header: 'Name',
            size: { flex: 2, minWidth: 140 },
            display: { pinned: 'left' },
            filter: { type: 'text' },
            edit: {
              enabled: true,
              type: 'text',
              validator: (value) =>
                !value || String(value).trim() === '' ? 'Name is required' : null,
            },
          },
          {
            field: 'department',
            header: 'Department',
            size: { flex: 1, minWidth: 110 },
            filter: { type: 'text' },
            edit: { enabled: true, type: 'dropdown', options: DEPARTMENTS },
          },
          {
            field: 'salary',
            header: 'Salary',
            size: { flex: 1, minWidth: 100 },
            filter: { type: 'number' },
            display: {
              formatter: (v) => `$${Number(v).toLocaleString()}`,
              exportFormatter: (v) => String(v),
              cellClass: (v) => (Number(v) > 90_000 ? 'salary-high' : ''),
            },
            // only active employees' salaries are editable
            edit: {
              enabled: (row) => row.active,
              type: 'number',
              min: 0,
              max: 1_000_000,
              parser: (raw) => Number(raw),
            },
          },
          {
            field: 'active',
            header: 'Active',
            size: { flex: 1, minWidth: 90 },
            filter: { type: 'boolean' },
            display: { formatter: (v) => (v ? '✓ Active' : '✗ Inactive') },
            edit: { enabled: true, type: 'boolean' },
          },
          {
            field: 'joinDate',
            header: 'Join Date',
            size: { flex: 1, minWidth: 120 },
            display: {
              formatter: (v) => (v ? new Date(v).toLocaleDateString() : '—'),
            },
            edit: {
              enabled: true,
              type: 'date',
              minDate: new Date('2010-01-01'),
              maxDate: new Date(),
            },
          },
        ],

        data: employees,

        sorting: { enabled: true, multiSort: true },
        filtering: { enabled: true },
        pagination: { enabled: true, pageSize: 25, pageSizeOptions: [25, 50, 100] },
        selection: { mode: 'multiple', selectAllScope: 'page' },
        editing: { enabled: true, trigger: 'doubleClick', moveOnTab: true },
        appearance: { rowHeight: 44, headerHeight: 48, rowStriping: true },
        accessibility: { gridLabel: 'Employee data grid', announceFocus: false },
        export: { filename: 'employees', scope: 'filtered' },

        events: {
          onEditCommit: (rowId, field, value) => {
            console.log(`Saved row ${rowId}: ${field} = ${value}`)
            // 👉 persist to your backend here
          },
        },
      })

      // ── 3. Build the API immediately — no need to wait for onReady ──────
      const api = buildGridAPI(grid)

      // ── 4. Wire up the custom toolbar ────────────────────────────────────
      const selectionCountEl = document.getElementById('selection-count')
      const exportSelectedBtn = document.getElementById('export-selected')
      const deleteSelectedBtn = document.getElementById('delete-selected')

      function renderSelection(state) {
        selectionCountEl.textContent = `${state.count} selected`
        exportSelectedBtn.disabled = state.count === 0
        deleteSelectedBtn.disabled = state.count === 0
      }

      renderSelection(grid.kernel.store.read('selection'))
      grid.kernel.store.subscribe('selection', renderSelection)

      document.getElementById('select-all').addEventListener('click', () => api.selectAll())
      document.getElementById('clear-selection').addEventListener('click', () => api.deselectAll())
      document.getElementById('export-selected').addEventListener('click', () =>
        api.exportCSV({ filename: 'selected', scope: 'selected' })
      )
      document.getElementById('delete-selected').addEventListener('click', () => {
        api.deleteRows([...api.getSelectedIds()])
        api.deselectAll()
      })
      document.getElementById('export-all').addEventListener('click', () => api.exportCSV())
      document.getElementById('clear-filters').addEventListener('click', () => api.clearFilters())

      // ── 5. Mount the grid ────────────────────────────────────────────────
      mount(grid, document.getElementById('grid-container'))
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

Reading the example top to bottom

If the file looks like a lot at once, here is the same code explained in plain English. It is organised into the five numbered sections from the comments.

① The data shape We first describe what one row looks like — an id, a name, a salary, and so on (shown as a comment above since this file is plain JavaScript; in a .ts file this would be a real interface Employee passed as createGrid<Employee>, which makes field: 'name' autocomplete and reject typos). The Array.from({ length: 200 }, …) line just fabricates 200 fake employees so there's something to scroll; in a real app this is the data you fetched from your server. (See Chapter 01.)

② Create the grid This is the big createGrid({ … }) call. Because vanilla JS has no re-render cycle, there's no hoisting concern to think about — see Chapter 01. Inside it, each column turns on the features from earlier chapters:

  • name is pinned left, text-filterable, and editable with a "required" validator (Ch 07).
  • salary is number-filtered, formatted as currency for display but exported as a plain number, colour-coded with cellClass, and editable only for active employees via the function form of edit.enabled (Ch 08, Ch 07).
  • active uses a boolean filter and a single-click boolean editor.
  • joinDate is formatted for humans and edited with a bounded date picker.

Below the columns, the grid-level groups (sorting, filtering, pagination, selection, editing, appearance, accessibility, export) switch on each feature. Every one of these has its own chapter if you want the details.

③ Build the API buildGridAPI(grid) gets us a fully working api object immediately — no need to wait for onReady since we're wiring up plain DOM buttons that already exist (Chapter 12).

④ Wire up the custom toolbar The selected-row count is read live by subscribing to the 'selection' namespace on grid.kernel.store — one small function replaces what would otherwise be its own hand-rolled bit of state tracking (Chapter 12). Every button in the toolbar just calls an API method (api.selectAll(), api.exportCSV(...), api.deleteRows(...)) — the pattern is the same everywhere: look up the element once, add a click listener, call the API inside it.

⑤ Mount the grid mount() draws the grid into the fixed-height <div class="grid-wrap"> (the grid fills its parent, so the parent must have a height).

That's the whole pattern: configure once, control via the API, mirror state via the store. Everything else is just which options you turn on.

What this example demonstrates

Feature Where
Typed columns createGrid<Employee> + field autocomplete (TypeScript projects)
Pinned column name → display.pinned: 'left'
Flexible widths size.flex + minWidth
Sorting (multi) sorting.multiSort
Filtering (per type) filter.type on each column
Pagination pagination group
Multiple selection selection.mode
Inline editing editing + per-column edit
Per-row editable salary.edit.enabled is a function
Validation name.edit.validator
Value formatting salary/active/joinDate formatters
Conditional styling salary.display.cellClass
CSV export (scopes) api.exportCSV(...)
Custom toolbar via API api.selectAll, deleteRows, clearFilters
Live selection count grid.kernel.store.subscribe('selection', ...)
Accessibility accessibility.gridLabel

That's the whole vanilla JS core. Go back to the manual index to revisit any chapter, or open the Glossary for definitions of any term used in this manual.

Next: 16 · Glossary

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.blurb: Plain-English definitions of every term used in this manual
chapters.html:
A plain-English dictionary of every term used in this manual. Skim it once, then come back whenever a word in another chapter is unfamiliar. Terms are grouped: EliteGrid concepts first, then general web/JavaScript terms, then vanilla JS/DOM terms.

EliteGrid concepts

Core (@elitegrid/core) The framework-agnostic engine every adapter — @elitegrid/react, @elitegrid/vue, and @elitegrid/vanilla — wraps internally. It has no dependency on React, Vue, or any framework and talks directly to the DOM, but you never install or import it yourself; even this manual documents @elitegrid/vanilla, not core directly (see Adapter, next).

Adapter A package that wraps the framework-agnostic core engine and exposes it in the shape natural to a given environment: @elitegrid/react adds a <Grid> component and hooks, @elitegrid/vue adds a <Grid> component and composables, and @elitegrid/vanilla — the one this manual documents — adds createGrid()/mount() for plain DOM usage. Every environment gets one; "no framework" doesn't mean "no adapter."

Core engine / kernel The "brain" that holds your data and runs sorting, filtering, pagination, selection, and editing. createGrid() builds one. mount() draws it on screen. Also called the engine or kernel, and reachable at grid.kernel.

createGrid(options) The function that builds the engine from your columns, data, and feature options. Returns a plain GridInstance object — call it once, wherever your script starts. (See Chapter 01.)

mount(grid, container) The function that draws the engine into a DOM element — the header, rows, scrollbars, and pagination bar. It fills its container, so the container needs a height. Returns a dispose function. (See Chapter 01.)

Dispose function The function mount() returns. Calling it removes the grid's DOM and view listeners; pass { destroyOnDispose: true } to mount() if you also want it to tear down the engine itself. (See Chapter 12.)

buildGridAPI(grid) Builds a Grid API object directly from a GridInstance, synchronously, any time — the alternative to waiting for onReady. (See Chapter 12.)

Grid API The "remote control" object full of methods (api.setPage(), api.exportCSV(), …) for driving the grid from your own code. Get it via buildGridAPI(grid) or the onReady event. (See Chapter 12.)

Event bus (grid.kernel.eventBus) The engine's internal publish/subscribe system. .on(event, handler) subscribes and returns an unsubscribe function; GridEvent is the enum of event names it emits. The events object passed to createGrid() is a friendlier layer on top of a subset of these. (See Chapter 11.)

Data store (grid.kernel.store) The engine's state container, split into namespaces (selection, paginated, sorted, …). .read(namespace) gives a one-off snapshot; .subscribe(namespace, callback) calls you back on every change and returns an unsubscribe function. The vanilla way to keep your own UI in sync with grid state. (See Chapter 12.)

Column definition (ColumnDef) One object in the columns array describing a single column. Uses grouped config: related settings live under size, display, sort, filter, edit, and value. (See Chapter 02.)

Grouped config EliteGrid's style of nesting a column's many settings into named groups so autocomplete stays tidy. size: { width: 80 } rather than a flat width: 80.

field The property name a column reads from each row (row.salary). It doubles as the column's unique ID in API calls. Every column needs a distinct field.

rowId Tells the grid which field uniquely identifies a row (defaults to id). Used to track selection, edits, and re-renders. Can be a field name or a function. (See Chapter 01.)

Pinning (freezing) Sticking a column to the left or right edge so it stays put while the rest scroll sideways — like "freeze panes" in a spreadsheet.

flex A column width that grows/shrinks to share leftover space, weighted against other flex columns (flex: 2 gets twice the share of flex: 1). The counterpart to a fixed pixel width.

Comparator A function (a, b) => number that decides the order of two values when sorting: negative if a comes first, positive if b does, 0 if equal. Used for custom sort orders. (See Chapter 03.)

Sort model An array of { columnId, direction } describing the current sort. The array order is the priority (primary sort first, then tie-breakers).

Operator The kind of comparison a filter performs: contains, equals, greater than, between, etc. Different data types offer different operators.

Filter model An object keyed by column field describing the active filters, each { type, operator, value }. (See Chapter 04.)

Popover The small floating panel anchored to the funnel icon that holds a column's filter controls.

Debounce Waiting until the user stops typing before reacting, so the grid filters once instead of on every keystroke. Controlled by filtering.debounceMs.

Page / page size A page is one screenful of rows; page size is how many rows per page. Pagination splits the data into pages with navigation controls. (See Chapter 05.)

Selection The grid's private list of which row IDs are currently ticked. Reading it lets you act on chosen rows (delete, export, etc.). Modes: none, single, multiple. (See Chapter 06.)

Inline editing Changing a cell's value in place — the cell becomes an input — rather than in a separate form. Has a start → commit → cancel lifecycle. (See Chapter 07.)

Parser An editor function that converts the raw string from an <input> into your data's real type (e.g. "42" → 42). Without it, number fields can end up as strings.

Validator An editor function that checks a typed value before saving. Return an error string to reject, or null to accept. May be async (return a Promise).

Formatter A display function that turns the underlying value into the display text (49.99 → "$49.99"). Affects only what's shown — sorting/filtering still use the real value.

exportFormatter A separate formatter used only for CSV export, for when the on-screen format is bad for spreadsheets ($50,000 → 50000).

Getter / setter (value group) A getter reads a value out of a row (for nested or computed columns); a setter writes one back (for editing nested data). (See Chapter 08.)

Pipeline The internal sequence your rows pass through: raw → filter → sort → paginate → displayed. getData() reads the start; getDisplayedRows() reads the end.

Virtualization Rendering only the rows visible in the viewport (plus a buffer) and recycling them as you scroll, so even a million rows stay fast. Always on. (See Chapter 14.)

Viewport The visible, scrollable window onto the data — usually a few dozen rows.

Buffer (scroll.bufferSize) Extra rows rendered just outside the viewport so scrolling doesn't flash blank.

dataSource An object with a getRows method used instead of data when rows are too large to load at once. The grid asks for one page at a time; your server does the filtering/sorting. (See Chapter 14.)

Announcement A short spoken message pushed to a screen reader when something changes ("Sorted by name, ascending"). Configurable and translatable. (See Chapter 13.)

Empty state / loading state / error state Full-grid overlays shown when there are no rows, while data is loading, or when a data source fails. (See Chapter 09.)

VanillaNode The type used for anything you hand the grid to render as an icon or overlay content: an HTMLElement, a plain string, or null/undefined. No render function or virtual DOM involved — build a real element and pass it in.

VanillaRenderer The type used for custom empty/loading/error UI (emptyStateComponent, loadingComponent, errorComponent): a plain function (container, ...args) => void that paints directly into the container element the grid gives it.

General web & JavaScript terms

TypeScript interface / type A description of an object's shape (its properties and their types). Exists only to help the compiler catch mistakes; produces no runtime code. Entirely optional — everything in this manual works in plain JavaScript too, just without the autocomplete.

Generic type argument (<Product>) Extra type information you pass to a function, e.g. createGrid<Product>(...), so it knows the shape of your data and can autocomplete and type-check. TypeScript-only.

Autocomplete / IntelliSense The dropdown of suggestions your editor shows as you type, powered by TypeScript types.

Callback / event handler A function you give to something else so it can call you back at the right moment (e.g. onRowClick). You define what happens; the grid decides when.

Signature The shape of a function's inputs and output, written as an arrow type, e.g. (row, event) => void. void means "returns nothing useful".

Async / Promise / await "Async" means a result arrives later, not immediately (e.g. a network request). A Promise is the placeholder for that future value; await pauses until it arrives.

Closure The bundle of surrounding variables a function "remembers" from when it was created. In vanilla JS, since a script only ever runs once, a closure over a let variable always sees the current value — there's no framework re-creating the function with a stale copy.

Immutability ("copy, don't mutate") Producing a new object with changes applied (often via the ... spread) instead of modifying the existing one. Helps the grid detect changes reliably.

DOM (Document Object Model) The browser's live tree of the HTML elements on the page. Each element costs memory and layout time, which is why virtualization keeps the count tiny.

CSS class A name attached to an element so a matching stylesheet rule styles it. cellClass attaches one to cells.

CSS custom property ("CSS variable") A reusable named value in CSS, starting with -- (e.g. --eg-accent). EliteGrid themes itself with these, all prefixed --eg-. Override them to re-skin the grid.

localStorage A small browser store for strings that survives page reloads. Used to remember things like saved column layouts (JSON.stringify to save, JSON.parse to read).

Serializable Able to be turned into a string (via JSON.stringify) and back, so it can be stored or sent over the network. The column-state object is serializable.

CSV (Comma-Separated Values) A plain-text table format — one line per row, cells separated by commas — that every spreadsheet program opens. (See Chapter 10.)

Delimiter The character placed between cells in a CSV (a comma by default; sometimes ; or a tab \t).

Set A JavaScript collection of unique values. getSelectedIds() returns one; spread it into an array ([...set]) to use array methods like .map.

ascending / descending Sort directions. Ascending (asc) goes small→large (A→Z, 0→9); descending (desc) is the reverse.

Locale The user's language/region setting. toLocaleString() formats numbers and dates to match it.

Accessibility terms

a11y Shorthand for accessibility ("a" + 11 letters + "y").

i18n Shorthand for internationalization ("i" + 18 letters + "n") — supporting multiple languages and regions.

Screen reader Software (VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS) that reads the interface aloud for blind and low-vision users.

ARIA HTML attributes (like role="grid", aria-label) that tell assistive technology what an element is and how it behaves.

Assistive technology (AT) Umbrella term for screen readers and similar tools.

prefers-reduced-motion A browser setting indicating the user wants less animation. EliteGrid honours it automatically.

Vanilla JS / DOM terms

<script type="module"> The modern way to load JavaScript that supports import/export directly in the browser, with no bundler required. Every code sample in this manual assumes ES module syntax.

document.getElementById / querySelector Standard DOM methods for finding an element already on the page, so you can pass it to mount() or attach event listeners.

addEventListener The standard DOM method for running a function when something happens to an element (a click, a keypress). The vanilla equivalent of a framework's @click/onClick prop — you wire it up by hand once, on the element itself.

DOMContentLoaded A browser event that fires once the initial HTML has been parsed, before images/styles finish loading. Useful for deferring a mount() call until a container element is guaranteed to exist.

Bundler A build tool (Vite, webpack, esbuild, …) that combines your JavaScript files and npm dependencies into files a browser can load efficiently. Optional — @elitegrid/vanilla also ships a browser-ready build for use without one.

Namespace (store) One named slice of grid.kernel.store's state — selection, paginated, sorted, and so on — each independently readable and subscribable. (See Chapter 12.)

Subscribe / unsubscribe Registering a callback to be called every time a piece of state changes (store.subscribe, eventBus.on), and the matching call to stop (unsubscribe(), off()). Always pair the two — an unsubscribe you never call is a small, permanent memory leak.

Back to the manual index.

chapters.title: Modules
chapters.blurb: Which features are opt-in, and what reaches your bundle
chapters.html:
Every feature in this manual is one of two kinds: mandatory — you get it whether you ask or not — or a module, which only exists in your app if you name it.

This chapter is short, and it is the one to read before the others. If a feature from another chapter does nothing when you try it, you are almost certainly missing its module, and this is the page that tells you which one.

The one-line version

If you want everything, and you do not want to think about it:

import { createGrid, AllModules, mount } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

const grid = createGrid<User>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
})

mount(grid, document.getElementById('grid')!)

That is the whole upgrade path from 0.1.x. AllModules behaves — and weighs — exactly the way the grid did before modules existed. Nothing in this chapter is work you must do; trimming the list is opt-in.

Coming from an older version? Before modules, createGrid({ columns, data }) gave you sorting, filtering, pagination, selection, editing and export automatically. It no longer does. Adding modules: [AllModules] restores that exactly. Every code sample in this manual includes a modules line for the same reason.

Why features are opt-in

A runtime flag like sorting: { enabled: false } turns a feature off. It does not remove the sorting code from the JavaScript your users download — the code still ships, it just sits there deciding not to run.

A module is different. SortModule is a value you import. If you never import it, the bundler can see that nothing references the sort plugin, and it drops the whole thing. That is a thing no flag can do.

The payoff is real and measured:

What you register Gzipped Saving
Everything ([AllModules]) 76.9 kB —
Nothing (modules: []) 55.5 kB 21.4 kB less

Both figures are gzipped, measured by the benchmark harness rather than estimated. Trimming to modules: [] saves you about 21 kB — worth having, and the reason the system exists, but notice that the grid is still 55.5 kB. That floor is the mandatory half, described below.

Jargon check — "tree-shaking": The bundler's ability to delete code nothing references. It only works when the bundler can prove the code is unused, which is why modules are plain values you import rather than strings you configure. A string like 'sort' tells the bundler nothing.

A note if you are using a <script> tag rather than a bundler. Tree-shaking is something your build tool does. If you load EliteGrid from a CDN as a prebuilt bundle, that file already contains everything and modules only selects which features are active — you get the behaviour benefits of this chapter but not the size ones. The size argument applies when you install from npm and build with Vite, Rollup, webpack or esbuild.

What you always get

Eight modules are mandatory. createGrid adds them itself, you cannot remove them, and you never name them:

Module Why it is not optional
DataSourceModule Holds your rows
RowModelModule Row identity — which row is which
ColumnModelModule Your column definitions
CellValueModule Resolves the value for every cell drawn
PipelineBridgeModule Connects raw → filtered → sorted → paginated
ViewportModule Virtualization and scrolling
FocusModule Keyboard navigation
AnnouncementModule Screen-reader announcements

The first six are structural: without rows, identity, columns, a viewport or cell-value resolution there is nothing to render at all.

The last two are a deliberate product decision rather than a technical limit. Focus and Announcement are as removable as Sort or Filter — but making accessibility opt-in means that in practice almost nobody opts in, and "the grid announces sort, filter and page changes to a screen reader" quietly stops being true for most installs. Keyboard navigation and screen-reader support are not features you should have to know to enable, so they are in the floor.

The modules you can register

import {
  createGrid,
  SortModule,
  FilterModule,
  SearchModule,
  GroupModule,
  PaginationModule,
  SelectionModule,
  EditModule,
  ExportModule,
  MenuModule,
  InfiniteScrollModule,
} from '@elitegrid/vanilla'
Module Turns on Chapter
SortModule Clicking a header to sort; sort arrows Sorting
FilterModule The funnel icon, filter popovers, floating filters Filtering
SearchModule Global quick-filter across all columns Filtering
GroupModule Row grouping, aggregation, group heading rows —
PaginationModule The pagination bar and page state Pagination
SelectionModule Checkboxes and row selection Row Selection
EditModule Double-click-to-edit and the cell editor Inline Editing
ExportModule api.exportCSV() and CSV generation Exporting to CSV
MenuModule The header ⋮ menu and the right-click context menu —
InfiniteScrollModule Load-as-you-scroll instead of pages —

AllModules contains the first nine. InfiniteScrollModule is deliberately not in it — see below.

Picking a list

Register what you use. A read-only report with sortable columns and a CSV button:

import { createGrid, SortModule, ExportModule, mount } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [SortModule, ExportModule],
  columns,
  data,
})

const dispose = mount(grid, document.getElementById('grid')!)

Order does not matter — each module sorts itself into the pipeline by its own internal priority, so you can list them however reads best.

A genuinely minimal grid is legal too. modules: [] gives you a scrolling, virtualized, keyboard-navigable, screen-reader-friendly table with no sort, filter, paging, selection, editing or export:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({ modules: [], columns, data })

When you forget one

This is the failure mode worth recognising, because the grid does not crash — a missing module hides its affordance rather than breaking. That is intentional: nothing renders a control that would silently do nothing.

You forgot What you see
SortModule Headers render, clicking one does nothing, no sort arrow
FilterModule No funnel icon anywhere
PaginationModule No pagination bar; every row on one page
SelectionModule No checkboxes, even with selection: { mode: 'multiple' }
EditModule Double-clicking a cell does nothing, even with edit configured
ExportModule api.exportCSV() is a no-op
MenuModule No ⋮ button and no right-click menu

So the diagnosis is always the same: the control I expected is not there → the module is not registered.

Import modules from the adapter, not from core

This one is worth care, because it is the only way to get a module that is half working. Several modules own a piece of UI — GroupModule owns the group heading row, EditModule the cell editor, PaginationModule the pagination bar, FilterModule the filter surfaces, MenuModule both menus. The copy that carries the renderer lives in @elitegrid/vanilla. @elitegrid/core exports a bare copy that registers the behaviour and renders nothing.

// ✅ correct — carries the DOM renderers
import { GroupModule, EditModule } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

// ❌ wrong — groups and edits correctly, renders no group rows and no editor
import { GroupModule, EditModule } from '@elitegrid/core'

You do not have to remember this, because the grid tells you in development:

[EliteGrid] GroupModule is registered but its "groupRow" component is missing,
so its output will not render. Import GroupModule from your adapter package
(@elitegrid/react, @elitegrid/vue, @elitegrid/vanilla) rather than from
@elitegrid/core — the adapter's copy is the one that carries the component.

The short rule: everything comes from @elitegrid/vanilla. You should never need to import from @elitegrid/core directly.

Two modules with a quirk

InfiniteScrollModule is not in AllModules

Infinite scroll and pagination are mutually exclusive — one replaces pages with endless scrolling, the other provides the pages. AllModules contains PaginationModule, so if it also contained InfiniteScrollModule every grid built with AllModules would warn about the conflict and then disable one of them.

It is also the kind of feature that must never switch on by surprise: an upgrade that silently turned a paginated server-side grid into an endlessly scrolling one would be a bug, not a gift. So you name it explicitly, and you drop pagination when you do:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [SortModule, InfiniteScrollModule],
  columns,
  dataSource,
  infiniteScroll: { pageSize: 100 },
})

MenuModule carries no behaviour

Every other module registers a plugin. MenuModule registers nothing — it exists purely as a bundling key for the column menu and the context menu renderers. Its only job is to let you leave two fairly large UI trees out of your bundle.

That means a hand-picked list must name it explicitly to keep the menus, even if you have configured them:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [SortModule, MenuModule], // without MenuModule, no ⋮ and no right-click menu
  columns,
  data,
  columnMenu: { enabled: true },
})

If you configure a menu without registering the module, you get a warning rather than silence:

[EliteGrid] The column menu and context menu need MenuModule, which is not
registered, so the ⋮ button and the right-click menu will not render. Add
MenuModule to `modules` (it is already in AllModules), or set
`columnMenu: { enabled: false }` to silence this.

Writing your own module

If you are building a package on top of EliteGrid and want to ship your own plugin, defineModule is the supported entry point:

import { createGrid, defineModule, defineBundle } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

const AuditModule = defineModule({
  id: 'audit-log',
  key: 'audit',
  order: 90,
  create: (ctx) => new AuditPlugin(ctx.options),
})

// Several of your own modules under one name
const MyGridBundle = defineBundle({
  id: 'my-company-grid',
  dependsOn: [SortModule, FilterModule, AuditModule],
})

const grid = createGrid<Row>({ modules: [MyGridBundle], columns, data })

Use withUI if your module also owns a renderer that the grid should pick up, the same way GroupModule supplies its group row.

One caveat if you care about bundle size in your own package: declare your bundles as object literals where you can. A call like defineBundle({ … }) at the top level of a file is something a bundler cannot prove is harmless, so it keeps the call — and keeping the call keeps everything you passed to it. This matters for library authors, not for application code.

Checklist

  • Want the old behaviour with no thought? modules: [AllModules].
  • A feature does nothing? Its module is not in your list.
  • A feature behaves but renders nothing? You imported it from @elitegrid/core instead of @elitegrid/vanilla.
  • Using the column or context menu with a hand-picked list? Add MenuModule.
  • Using infinite scroll? Name InfiniteScrollModule and drop PaginationModule.
  • Keyboard navigation and screen-reader support need no module and cannot be removed.

Next: Columns covers what you can do with a column definition.

chapters.title: Row Grouping & Aggregation
chapters.blurb: Sections, aggregates, grand totals, sticky headings
chapters.html:
Grouping collapses rows that share a value into expandable sections — all invoices for a customer, all employees in a department — and puts a summary on each section heading.

Two features that ship together, because grouping without totals is half a feature:

  • Grouping builds the sections.
  • Aggregation computes the number on each heading — a sum, an average, your own function.

Requires GroupModule. Grouping adds a pipeline stage and a store namespace, so it is a real module in the original sense. Without it, grouping is ignored entirely and no section headings render. See Modules.

The smallest grouped grid

import { createGrid, GroupModule, mount } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [GroupModule],
  columns,
  data: invoices,
  grouping: {
    model: ['customer'],
  },
})

mount(grid, document.getElementById('grid')!)

model is the list of columns to group by, outermost first. Two entries means two levels:

grouping: {
  model: ['region', 'customer'], // every customer nested inside its region
}

You can pass the ColumnDef object instead of the field name. Both are type-checked and both follow a rename:

const regionColumn = { field: 'region', header: 'Region' }

grouping: { model: [regionColumn, 'customer'] }

An entry that matches no column warns by name in development rather than silently grouping by nothing.

The column you group by disappears

This is the first surprise, and it is deliberate. Grouping by Customer hides the Customer column, because the value is already in the section heading — showing it again puts the same string on every row of the section.

If you want it back:

grouping: {
  model: ['customer'],
  keepGroupedColumns: true,
}

Why this is the default: a grouped column left visible shows every row its own group's value twice — the group label above it, the same value again in the cell. Hiding it is the behaviour nearly everyone wants, so it is the default, with one flag to opt out.

Aggregation — the number on the heading

A column shows nothing on a group row unless you tell it what to compute. Set value.aggregate on the column:

const columns: ColumnDef<Invoice>[] = [
  { field: 'customer', header: 'Customer' },
  {
    field: 'amount',
    header: 'Amount',
    value: { aggregate: 'sum' },
  },
  {
    field: 'daysLate',
    header: 'Days Late',
    value: { aggregate: 'avg' },
  },
]

Seven built-in names: 'sum', 'avg', 'min', 'max', 'count', 'first', 'last'.

A column with no aggregate renders blank on a group row — never the first child's value. That is a safety decision. Showing the first row's amount on a heading is how a reader comes to believe a group of 12 invoices is worth $2,400.

Your own aggregate

Pass a function instead. It receives the extracted values and the typed rows, because most real aggregates need a sibling field:

{
  field: 'amount',
  header: 'Amount',
  value: {
    // a weighted average needs the weight column
    aggregate: (values, rows) => {
      const totalWeight = rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.weight, 0)
      if (totalWeight === 0) return 0
      return rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.amount * r.weight, 0) / totalWeight
    },
  },
}
// "how many in this group are overdue"
value: { aggregate: (values, rows) => rows.filter((r) => r.overdue).length }

A typo in a built-in name is a compile error, not a blank cell — the names are a union resolved by a switch, not a string looked up in a registry at runtime.

There is no aggregate formatter, on purpose. display.formatter receives a TData row, and a group row is not one. If you want control over how an aggregate is displayed, return a string from a custom aggregate — that is the supported path.

Aggregates are computed from the leaves at every level, never folded up from the level below. Folding is wrong for any non-associative function: an avg over unequal group sizes, or any custom median, comes out wrong.

A grand total over everything

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  grandTotal: 'bottom', // or 'top'
}

The grand total is a pinned row, so it stays visible while you scroll, and it re-totals whenever a filter changes. It works with an empty model too — a totals row on an ungrouped grid:

grouping: { model: [], grandTotal: 'top' }

Controlling the group key

By default a group's key is the column's display value — the same text search and tooltips read. So a column shown as $1,234 groups as $1,234, and a formatter that maps a status code to a label groups by the label, with nothing written.

Two cases the default gets wrong, and both warn in development:

A cellRenderer column — a rendered node has no text to group on.

A Date column — every distinct instant becomes its own group, which is never what you want. Bucket it:

{
  field: 'issuedAt',
  header: 'Issued',
  group: {
    valueGetter: (row) => String(row.issuedAt.getFullYear()),
  },
}

Ordering the sections

{
  field: 'priority',
  header: 'Priority',
  group: {
    comparator: (a, b) => RANK[a] - RANK[b], // 'high' before 'low'
  },
}

group.comparator orders the sections. sort.comparator orders the rows inside a section. They are independent, and the distinction matters:

  • Sorting the grid by a grouped column flips the section order.
  • Sorting by any other column reorders rows inside each section and leaves the section order alone.

The default section order is a numeric-aware locale compare, so Item 2 sorts before Item 10.

Blocking the menu affordance

{ field: 'notes', header: 'Notes', group: { enabled: false } }

That removes "Group by this column" from the column menu. Grouping it programmatically still works — this gates the affordance, not the capability.

How the sections look

One column, or the full width

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  displayType: 'singleColumn', // default
  groupColumn: { header: 'Region', width: 220, minWidth: 120 },
}

'singleColumn' prepends one synthetic column holding the chevron, the key and the count, indented by depth. 'fullWidth' spans the heading across every column and leaves your data columns alone.

What starts open

grouping: {
  model: ['region', 'customer'],
  expandedByDefault: 1, // top level only
}

false (the default) starts everything closed, true everything open, and a number opens to that depth.

Counts

grouping: { model: ['region'], showCounts: false } // drop the "(12)"

Sticky headings

As you scroll inside a section its heading pins under the column header, and the end of its own section pushes it out. On by default — a feature nobody enables is a feature nobody has, and it costs nothing on a grid with one group.

Nested headings stack: at depth 2 both levels stay pinned, outermost above.

grouping: { model: ['region'], stickyGroups: false } // turn it off

The chip bar

A bar above the column header naming what you are grouped by, outermost first. Drag a chip to reorder a level, × to remove one.

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  panel: 'whenGrouped', // default — appears only once something is grouped
}

true keeps it always visible, false never. The default is 'whenGrouped' because the bar takes no column dropped onto it — an empty one cannot teach you to group, so it should not occupy space pretending to. Creating a grouping is the column menu's "Group by this column".

Collapsed sections that still say something

A collapsed section is a summary, not a dead end. collapsedPreview puts something behind the heading's label:

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  collapsedPreview: 'share',
}

'share' paints a faint proportion bar — this section's rows against the filtered total. It costs zero horizontal space, and the eye ranks the sections before reading a single number.

Or render anything you like:

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  collapsedPreview: ({ leafRows, share }) => {
    const el = document.createElement('div')
    el.className = 'yg-my-preview'
    el.style.opacity = share < 0.1 ? '0.4' : '1'
    el.textContent = leafRows.slice(0, 5).map((r) => r.owner).join(', ')
    return el
  },
}

leafRows is this section's filtered rows, and share is leafRows.length over the filtered total as a 0–1 number — handed to you so a custom preview paints the same proportion without re-deriving the denominator and getting it wrong.

Off by default.

Replacing the heading cell

grouping: {
  model: ['region'],
  cellRenderer: ({ group, label, toggle }) => {
    const el = document.createElement('button')
    el.className = 'yg-my-heading'
    el.textContent = `${group.expanded ? '▾' : '▸'} ${label} — ${group.count} rows`
    el.addEventListener('click', toggle)
    return el
  },
}
params What it is
label e.g. "Acme Corp (12)" — already honours showCounts and the locale
toggle() Expand or collapse this section
group.path Ordered keys from the root: ['EMEA', 'Acme Corp']
group.key This level's key — the last element of path
group.level 0 for a top-level section; -1 for the grand total
group.count Descendant row count, after filtering
group.aggregates Aggregate values by column id
group.expanded Current state
group.leaves Every descendant row

Selection

A group's checkbox selects everything under it, and the heading shows a tri-state box (checked / unchecked / partial) that follows its children:

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [GroupModule, SelectionModule],
  columns,
  data: invoices,
  selection: { mode: 'multiple' },
  grouping: { model: ['customer'], selectsChildren: true }, // default
})

With selectsChildren: false the checkbox is hidden, not disabled. A group row is not in the row model, so it cannot be selected as a thing in its own right — with its children off the table the box would be inert, and an inert checkbox is worse than none. The slot stays reserved so no cell shifts out from under its header.

Pagination

grouping: {
  model: ['customer'],
  paginateBy: 'rows', // default
}
  • 'rows' pages what the user actually sees, so the scrollbar and the row count stay honest. A section may straddle a page boundary.
  • 'groups' pages whole top-level sections — "25 customers per page".

Filtering a grouped grid

Nothing to configure, but worth knowing: the grouping stage runs after filter and search. Sections are built only from rows that survived them, which means an empty section cannot exist, counts always mean surviving rows, and there is no stale parent left behind.

Export

By default a CSV contains your rows, not your section headings — a spreadsheet user re-groups with a pivot table, and a file with summary rows interleaved is not a dataset.

grouping: { model: ['region'], exportGroups: true } // include the headings

Two things that are handled for you, and are worth knowing because the obvious expectation is wrong:

  • The columns you grouped by are always in the file, even though grouping hides them on screen. Hiding is a display decision, and a CSV has no headings to carry the value instead — a grid grouped by Department used to export a file with no Department column, carrying its grouping in row order alone.
  • An export does not depend on which sections are expanded. Rows come out in display order but not display membership, so collapsing everything does not produce a file of headings and no rows.

Driving it from code

api.setGroupModel(['region', 'customer']) // group, outermost first
api.setGroupModel([])                     // ungroup
api.getGroupModel()                       // [] when nothing is grouped

api.setGroupExpanded(['EMEA', 'Acme Corp'], true)
api.expandAllGroups()
api.collapseAllGroups()

A path is a plain string array, so it survives JSON and a page reload — which is what lets grid state restore which sections were open.

Events

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [GroupModule],
  columns,
  data: invoices,
  grouping: { model: ['region'] },
  events: {
    onGroupModelChange: (model) => console.log('grouped by', model),
    onGroupExpand: (path, expanded) => console.log(path, expanded),
  },
})

Gotchas

  • A group row is not one of your rows. It is a tagged object in the same flat list. If you write a custom renderer that walks rows, narrow with isGroupRow(row) before assuming you have a TData. Your own rows are untouched and still passed by reference.
  • A column with no value.aggregate is blank on a heading. That is intentional; see above.
  • Date and cellRenderer columns need group.valueGetter. Both warn in development.
  • keepGroupedColumns is false by default — the column you grouped by vanishes until you ask for it back.
  • exportGroups is false by default — headings are not in your CSV unless you ask.
  • GroupModule must come from @elitegrid/vanilla, not @elitegrid/core. Core's copy groups correctly and renders no headings at all. It warns if you get this wrong.

Next: Row Features covers pinned rows, row numbers, drag-to-reorder and expandable detail rows.

chapters.title: Row Features
chapters.blurb: Pinned rows, row numbers, auto-height, detail rows, drag to reorder
chapters.html:
Five things you can do to a row that are not sorting, filtering or editing it:

Feature What it does Module
Pinned rows Freeze rows above or below the scrolling body none
Row numbers An ordinal strip down the left edge none
Auto-height Rows that grow to fit their content none
Detail rows A row expands to reveal a panel none
Drag to reorder Drag a row somewhere else in the list none

None of them needs a module. They ride on ViewportPlugin, which is mandatory, so they all work on a grid built with modules: [].

Pinned top and bottom rows

Rows frozen above or below the scrolling body:

const grid = createGrid<Employee>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data: employees,
  pinnedRows: {
    top: [{ id: 'hdr', name: 'Engineering', salary: 0 }],
    bottom: [summaryRow],
  },
})

They are the same TData shape as a body row, which means every column option you already wrote — display.formatter, display.cellRenderer, display.tooltip — works on them unchanged.

A pinned row is presentation, not data. It is not in the row model, so it is never filtered, sorted, paginated, selected, focused, edited, exported or copied, and api.getData() does not include it. That is one rule covering every question you might have about how pinned rows interact with anything else: they don't.

Change them at runtime:

api.setPinnedRows('bottom', [newSummary])
api.setPinnedRows('top', []) // clear

For a totals row, do not build one here. Set grouping.grandTotal and let value.aggregate compute it — that row is pinned too, and it re-totals on every filter. See Row Grouping.

Row numbers

An automatic ordinal strip down the left edge, left of the selection checkbox:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({ modules: [], columns, data, rowNumbers: true })

true means "every default". There is no rowNumbers.enabled — the option's presence is the enable.

rowNumbers: {
  count: 'result', // default
  start: 1,        // default; 0 gives 0-based numbering
  width: 56,       // default — five digits at the default font
  header: '#',     // default comes from the locale
}

Which ordinal

This is the part worth choosing deliberately:

count Meaning
'result' (default) Position in the filtered + sorted result, running continuously across pages — page 3 of 20 starts at 41
'page' Restarts at 1 on every page
'source' Position in the original data array — immune to filter, search, sort and pagination

Naming these three is the feature: without them, every developer who cares about the difference ends up writing the same function.

Custom text

rowNumbers: {
  format: ({ row, index }) => `${row.department}-${index}`,
}

params.row is your own TData, not an any you have to cast.

It is not a column. The strip is never in columns.definitions, so it is never sorted, filtered, resized, pinned, reordered, hidden, focused, exported, or saved into a grid state view. If you need any of those, you want a real column with a valueGetter, not this.

Rows that size themselves

Every row is appearance.rowHeight (default 40) until something asks for more. Set display.wrap on a column and that column's text wraps, the row grows to fit, and rowHeight becomes the minimum rather than the fixed height:

const columns: ColumnDef<Ticket>[] = [
  { field: 'title', header: 'Title' },
  { field: 'description', header: 'Description', display: { wrap: true } },
]

Capping it

appearance: {
  rowHeight: 40,
  maxRowHeight: 160,
}

Uncapped is the default on purpose: a cap silently clips content, which is worse than one tall row. Instead, development mode warns once the first time a row exceeds 10× rowHeight and points you here.

Per-row control

appearance: {
  getRowHeight: (params) => {
    if (params.kind === 'group') return 32
    return params.row.pinned ? 72 : undefined // undefined = let the grid decide
  },
}

params is a discriminated union — { kind: 'row', row } or { kind: 'group', group } — so the group-row case is a branch the compiler makes you handle.

Called for every row of the display list, so keep it synchronous and cheap.

From code

api.setRowHeight('row-42', 120)
api.setRowHeight('row-42', null) // back to automatic
api.resetRowHeights()

One call — there is no separate refresh to remember afterwards.

Expandable detail rows

A row expands to reveal a panel underneath it. Supplying renderer is what turns the feature on — there is no rowDetail.enabled:

const grid = createGrid<Order>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data: orders,
  rowDetail: {
    renderer: ({ row }) => {
      const el = document.createElement('div')
      el.className = 'p-4'

      const title = document.createElement('h4')
      title.textContent = row.customer

      el.append(title, renderLineItems(row.items))
      return el
    },
  },
})

params.row is your own TData, and the return type is an HTMLElement — neither of them is any.

rowDetail: {
  renderer: ({ row }) => renderOrderDetail(row),

  // Which rows can expand. Default: all of them.
  isExpandable: (row) => row.items.length > 0,

  // Rows open on first render, by row id.
  defaultExpanded: ['order-1'],

  // At most one row open at a time. Opening a second closes the first.
  single: true,

  // Where the chevron goes. Default 'first-column'.
  toggle: 'first-column',

  // Assumed panel height until it has been measured. Default 200.
  estimatedHeight: 240,
}

estimatedHeight is an estimate, not a setting

The grid needs some number to lay out with before your panel exists — it is your component, so there is no string to measure. Once the panel paints, the auto-height pass measures it and corrects the row. Setting this near the real height means the grid never visibly corrects; leaving it means one small correction the first time a row opens.

One number, and it self-corrects — there is no second "measure instead" switch to find.

Driving it from code

api.expandRow('order-1')
api.collapseRow('order-1')
api.toggleRowExpanded('order-1')
api.isRowExpanded('order-1')
api.getExpandedRows()
api.expandAllRows()
api.collapseAllRows()

It is toggleRowExpanded, not toggleRow. toggleRow is taken — it toggles row selection. Two different things called "toggling a row" is exactly the ambiguity the longer name buys out.

All of these are synchronous and take the same row id string as setRowHeight and flashCells. The three opening calls warn in development if the feature is off or the row is not expandable; the two closing calls stay silent, because asking to close something already closed got the outcome it asked for.

expandAllRows() warns past about 1,000 rows rather than refusing — on a filtered set of 20 it is reasonable, on 100k it almost certainly is not, and the call cannot tell them apart.

Your own chevron

rowDetail: {
  renderer: ({ row }) => renderOrderDetail(row),
  toggle: 'none',
}

// then, in a column:
{
  field: 'customer',
  header: 'Customer',
  display: {
    cellRenderer: ({ row }) => {
      const el = document.createElement('button')
      el.textContent = row.customer
      el.addEventListener('click', () => api.toggleRowExpanded(String(row.id)))
      return el
    },
  },
}

toggle: 'none' is the escape hatch, not the default — configuring it and then never calling toggleRowExpanded() warns in development.

Drag to reorder

const grid = createGrid<Task>({ modules: [], columns, data, rowDrag: true })

That is the whole configuration for the common case.

rowDrag: {
  // Where the grip lives. Default 'first-column'.
  //   'first-column'       inside the first visible column's cells
  //   'row'                the whole row is draggable
  //   { column: 'name' }   a specific column
  handle: 'first-column',

  isDraggable: (row) => !row.locked,
  canDrop: ({ row, target }) => target.status === row.status,
  whenSorted: 'disable', // or 'clear-sort'
  dragPreview: ({ row }) => pill(row.title), // null for none
}

It works filtered, sorted and paged

Worth stating plainly, because the competing implementation does not: a drop is resolved against the neighbour you dropped on, not against a display index. So dragging works on a filtered list and across pages.

When a sort is active

The one case with no good answer, so it is a choice you make:

  • 'disable' (default) — the handle renders disabled, with a localized tooltip saying why.
  • 'clear-sort' — freezes the visible order into the data and drops the sort. This is the only reading under which the gesture does what it looked like it did.

A development warning names this option the first time it bites.

The drag preview

What follows the pointer. The default is a pill showing the row's first visible cell — on touch, the row under the finger is the row you cannot see. Return null for no preview.

From code

api.moveRow('task-3', 0)                     // to the top
api.moveRows(['task-3', 'task-9'], 5)

Reacting to a reorder

events: {
  onRowOrderChanged: ({ source }) => {
    // `source` says whether this was a drag or an api.moveRow() call
    persistOrder(api.getData())
  },
}

Gotchas

  • Pinned rows are invisible to everything else — no filter, sort, selection, export or getData(). If you need a row to participate, it belongs in data.
  • rowNumbers is a strip, not a column. Nothing that works on columns works on it.
  • maxRowHeight is uncapped by default, and a cap clips. Prefer the warning.
  • getRowHeight must handle the 'group' branch — the compiler will tell you.
  • rowDetail.renderer is the enable. No renderer, no feature, and every expansion API call is a no-op.
  • toggleRowExpanded ≠ toggleRow. The short name is selection.
  • A drag under an active sort does nothing by default. Set whenSorted: 'clear-sort' if the gesture should win.

Next: 09 · Appearance & Theming
