It works filtered, sorted and paged

chapters.title: Menus & Clipboard
chapters.blurb: The column menu, right-click menu, and copy to clipboard
chapters.html:
Three features that share a theme — getting data and commands out of the grid without writing a toolbar:

  • The column menu — the ⋮ button in a column header.
  • The context menu — right-click in the body.
  • Clipboard copy — Ctrl/Cmd+C, and the API behind it.

The two menus need MenuModule, which carries no behaviour of its own — it exists purely so the two menu component trees can be left out of a bundle that does not want them. It is in AllModules. Clipboard copy needs no module at all.

Configure a menu without registering MenuModule and you get a development warning rather than silence.

The column menu

On by default wherever MenuModule is registered:

import { createGrid, AllModules, mount } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

const grid = createGrid<Invoice>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  columnMenu: {
    enabled: true,      // default
    showOnHover: false, // default — the ⋮ is always visible
    showColumnChooser: true, // default
  },
})
Option Default Meaning
enabled true Show the ⋮ button at all
showOnHover false Reveal the button only while the header is hovered
icon ⋮ Replace the glyph with your own node
showColumnChooser true The inline checkbox list of every column
items — Rewrite the item list

Keyboard focus and an open menu reveal the button regardless of showOnHover, so it is never unreachable.

Turning showColumnChooser off while the menu still offers "Hide column" warns in development — a hidden column would then have no route back.

What is in it

Item id What it does
sortAsc / sortDesc / clearSort Sorting
filter Opens this column's filter
groupBy / ungroup Row grouping
pinLeft / pinRight / unpin Column pinning
autoSizeThis / autoSizeAll Column auto-size
hide Hide this column
columns The inline column chooser

Each item appears only when the module behind it is registered — no SortModule, no sort items.

Rewriting the items

columnMenu: {
  items: ({ column, columnId, defaultItems, api }) => [
    ...defaultItems.filter((i) => i.id !== 'hide'),
    {
      id: 'copy-column',
      label: `Copy all of ${column.header}`,
      separator: true,
      action: () => api.copyToClipboard({ columns: [columnId], scope: 'filtered' }),
    },
  ],
}

defaultItems holds real objects with live actions, so both of these work:

defaultItems.filter((i) => i.id !== 'hide')        // drop one
defaultItems.map((i) => i.id === 'sortAsc' ? { ...i, label: 'A→Z' } : i)  // rename one

An item takes:

Field Meaning
id A built-in id, or any string for your own
label The text
icon Your own node
disabled Greyed out, with aria-disabled
checked Draws a check and makes it a radio row. undefined ≠ false — undefined means "no checked state"
separator Draw a rule above this item
action(params) What it does

separator lives on the item rather than being its own array entry, so filtering defaultItems can never strand a separator at the top or bottom of the menu.

Per-column tweaks

{
  field: 'notes',
  header: 'Notes',
  menu: {
    enabled: true,
    items: ({ defaultItems }) => defaultItems.filter((i) => i.id !== 'groupBy'),
  },
}

The grid-level columnMenu.items runs first, and the per-column menu.items runs on its output — so a grid-wide addition and a per-column tweak compose instead of one silently replacing the other.

The context menu

Right-click in the body:

contextMenu: {
  enabled: true,                // default — governs the BODY
  openColumnMenuOnHeader: true, // default
}
Item id Needs
copy / copyWithHeaders nothing
export / exportSelection ExportModule
expandAll / collapseAll GroupModule or rowDetail
autoSizeAll nothing
moveToTop / moveToBottom rowDrag

copy and autoSizeAll are ungated, so a grid built with modules: [] still gets a working right-click menu.

The browser's menu

When enabled is false the browser's own menu appears, because the grid suppresses it only when it shows its own. That one rule is the whole of the configuration.

Returning [] from items does the same thing, per target:

contextMenu: {
  items: ({ target, defaultItems }) =>
    target.kind === 'blank' ? [] : defaultItems, // browser menu outside cells
}

Right-clicking a header

openColumnMenuOnHeader (default true) opens that column's ⋮ menu at the pointer instead of the context menu. It is independent of enabled, which governs the body — a grid can legitimately want one and not the other.

The target

contextMenu: {
  items: ({ target, defaultItems, api }) => {
    if (target.kind === 'blank') return defaultItems
    return [
      ...defaultItems,
      {
        id: 'open',
        label: `Open ${target.row.customer}`,
        separator: true,
        action: () => router.push(`/invoices/${target.rowId}`),
      },
    ]
  },
}

target.kind is 'cell' or 'blank'. On a cell you get row (a real TData, by reference, never a group row), rowId, columnId and column.

Per-column context items

{
  field: 'secret',
  header: 'Secret',
  menu: {
    contextItems: () => [], // browser's menu over this column
  },
}

Named contextItems rather than a second items because both live in one group.

Opening it yourself

api.showContextMenu({ x: event.clientX, y: event.clientY })

Viewport coordinates — the same numbers a MouseEvent carries. That is the whole binding for a long-press on touch, a toolbar button or a custom keybinding.

This is deliberately not gated on contextMenu.enabled: a developer who turned the built-in right-click off and bound their own gesture is exactly the caller this method has. enabled governs the gesture the grid owns, not the feature.

Clipboard copy

Ctrl/Cmd+C copies the selection, or the focused cell if nothing is selected. On by default — copying what you selected is baseline behaviour, not a feature you opt into.

clipboard: {
  enabled: true,          // default — governs the SHORTCUT only
  includeHeaders: false,  // default
  delimiter: '\t',        // default
}

The default delimiter is a tab, because Excel, Sheets and Numbers all parse tab-separated paste into cells. A comma produces a single column in all three.

includeHeaders is off because a one-cell copy with a header line above it is wrong far more often than it is right — and a single focused cell never gets one regardless of the setting.

enabled: false disables the shortcut, not the feature. api.copyToClipboard() keeps working, because an API call is an explicit request rather than an affordance the grid offered.

From code

const result = await api.copyToClipboard({
  scope: 'selected',       // 'auto' | 'focused' | 'all' | 'filtered' | 'page' | 'selected'
  includeHeaders: true,
  columns: ['name', 'amount'],
  delimiter: ',',
})

if (!result.ok) {
  toast(result.reason === 'denied' ? 'Clipboard blocked' : 'Nothing to copy')
}

It returns a result rather than void:

Field Meaning
ok false when nothing was copied — the clipboard is left untouched, never overwritten with an empty string
text Exactly what was written, header row included
rowCount Rows written, excluding the header. A one-cell copy is 1 × 1
columnCount Columns written
reason Only when ok is false
reason Cause
'empty' Nothing selected, no focused cell, or no columns resolved
'unavailable' No clipboard host — server-side rendering, or a call before mount
'denied' The browser blocked it: non-secure context, denied permission, or no user gesture

Every copy method returns a result, so a clipboard write that the browser refuses is something you can see and handle rather than a silent no-op.

Gotchas

  • Both menus need MenuModule. It is in AllModules; a hand-picked list must name it. Configuring a menu without it warns.
  • columnMenu.items runs before column.menu.items, and the per-column one receives the output of the grid-level one.
  • checked: undefined is not checked: false. Undefined means the item has no checked state at all and stays a plain menuitem.
  • A menu item's separator draws a rule above itself, so filtering items never strands one.
  • clipboard.enabled: false still leaves api.copyToClipboard() working.
  • copyToClipboard can fail for reasons that are not your bug — a non-secure context or a missing user gesture. Check result.ok.
  • Floating menus portal to document.body, so they carry the grid's theme classes with them. If you are building your own floating surface, do the same or it will render light on a dark grid.

Next: Live & Streaming Data.

chapters.title: Live & Streaming Data
chapters.blurb: Transactions, infinite scroll, cell flash
chapters.html:
Three features for a grid whose data arrives while the user is looking at it:

  • Transactions — many row changes in one repaint.
  • Infinite scroll — fetch the next page as the user nears the bottom.
  • Cell flash — briefly highlight what just changed.

Transactions

Calling addRow() 500 times runs the whole pipeline 500 times. A transaction is many mutations in one pipeline pass and one repaint:

const result = api.applyTransaction({
  add: [newOrder],
  update: [{ id: 7, price: 19.99 }],
  remove: ['order-3', 'order-4'],
})

Needs no module and no configuration.

Field Takes
add Rows to insert
addIndex Where to insert — an index after removals are applied. Omit to append
update Partial<TData> changes, merged onto the existing row
remove Row ids — an array or a Set

update merges, it does not replace

A delta feed sends { id, price } and the row's other fields survive:

// row was { id: 7, name: 'Widget', price: 10, stock: 4 }
api.applyTransaction({ update: [{ id: 7, price: 12 }] })
// row is now { id: 7, name: 'Widget', price: 12, stock: 4 }

Each entry must carry enough for the configured rowId to resolve it — the id field for rowId: 'field', or every field the function reads for rowId: (row) => …. Entries that cannot be resolved are skipped and reported, not guessed at.

A partial update is a patch, not a replacement — you send the fields that changed, not the whole row.

remove takes ids

api.applyTransaction({ remove: api.getSelectedIds() })

That is the single most likely call anyone writes, so a Set is accepted as well as an array. A bare string is deliberately not accepted — remove: 'row-1' would otherwise iterate into deleting rows 'r', 'o', 'w'…

The result tells you what happened

const result = api.applyTransaction({ update: feed })

if (result.skipped.length > 0) {
  console.warn('feed ids have drifted', result.skipped)
}
Field Meaning
added Rows actually inserted, in insertion order
updated Rows after the merge — not the partials you passed
removed Rows as they were immediately before deletion
skipped Ops that were dropped, and why. Empty on a clean transaction
applied true when at least one row changed

applied is not the same as skipped.length === 0 — a transaction can add two rows and skip a third.

A skip carries { op, id?, reason, index }, where reason is one of:

reason Cause
'duplicate-id' add: a row with this id is already in the grid
'unknown-id' update / remove: no row with this id
'unresolvable-id' update: the configured rowId could not derive an id from the partial
'invalid-entry' remove: not a string. add / update: not an object

An update for an unknown id is reported rather than dropped — a feed whose ids have drifted should not go unnoticed for a week.

A busy feed

If messages arrive faster than you want to repaint, coalesce them:

const grid = createGrid<Tick>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data,
  transactions: { waitMs: 50 }, // default
})

socket.on('tick', (t) => {
  api.applyTransactionAsync({ update: [t] })
})

applyTransactionAsync returns a promise resolving to the same TransactionResult, and never rejects.

The timer is one per window, not per call: message 500 does not reset the clock message 1 started, so a busy feed still flushes every waitMs instead of being starved indefinitely.

api.flushTransactions() // apply everything queued, now

You only need flushTransactions() when your own code must see the rows — before a screenshot, a print, or a route change. A synchronous applyTransaction() flushes the queue first on its own.

Before mount and during server-side rendering there is no timer, so an async transaction applies immediately and resolves with the same result. Nothing is lost but the coalescing.

The event

events: {
  onTransaction: (result) => console.log(result.added.length, 'added'),
}

Fires once per applied applyTransaction(), after the pipeline settles — so api.getDisplayedRows() inside it is fresh. A transaction that changed nothing does not fire it.

onRowAdd / onRowUpdate / onRowDelete still fire per row for the same transaction, deliberately: suppressing them would mean a developer who wired onRowDelete sees nothing when a transaction deletes.

Infinite scroll

"Load 100 rows, then fetch the next 100 as the user nears the bottom" — no pagination bar.

import { createGrid, InfiniteScrollModule, mount } from '@elitegrid/vanilla'

const dataSource = {
  async getRows({ page, pageSize, sortModel, filterModel, search }) {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/orders?page=${page}&size=${pageSize}`)
    const { rows, total } = await res.json()
    return { rows, totalCount: total }
  },
}

const grid = createGrid<Order>({
  modules: [InfiniteScrollModule],
  columns,
  dataSource,
  infiniteScroll: {
    threshold: 20, // default — rows of lead time before the next fetch
    pageSize: 100, // defaults to pagination.pageSize, then to 100
  },
})

Two requirements:

  • dataSource, not data.
  • InfiniteScrollModule, named explicitly. It is deliberately not in AllModules, because it is mutually exclusive with PaginationModule — and because an upgrade that silently turned a server-paginated grid into an endlessly scrolling one would be a bug, not a gift.

pageSize is deliberately the same key the grid already has rather than a second "block size" concept — a developer who set pagination.pageSize: 100 and then switched to infinite scroll should not have to discover a new name for the number they already chose.

Two keys, and no second datasource interface. There is no cache to evict, no overflow to size and no concurrency to cap, because the loaded region is contiguous rather than sparse.

Driving and observing it

await api.loadMore()   // fetch the next page now
api.hasMoreRows()      // false once totalCount is reached
events: {
  onLoadMore: ({ page, loadedCount, totalCount }) =>
    console.log(`${loadedCount} / ${totalCount}`),

  onLoadMoreError: ({ error, page }) => {
    toast(`Page ${page} failed`)
  },
}

When a fetch fails

The rows already loaded stay on screen, and api.loadMore() is the retry:

events: {
  onLoadMoreError: ({ error }) => {
    showRetryBanner(() => api.loadMore())
  },
}

The failure path takes the error, keeps the block retryable, and says so in the UI — a page that failed to load is not a page that is permanently blank.

Filtering and sorting

sortModel, filterModel and search are all handed to getRows so a server-side source can honour them. A change to any of the three discards the loaded pages and refetches from page 1, because rows 0–299 sorted here and rows 300+ ordered by the server would not agree.

Honouring them server-side is about which rows you get, not about who orders them. The grid still sorts the rows it holds; there is no mode that defers ordering to the data source. A source that ignores sortModel returns later pages from an unsorted set, which reads as correct within a page and wrong across pages.

Cell flash

Briefly highlight a cell whose value changed:

const grid = createGrid<Tick>({
  modules: [],
  columns,
  data,
  appearance: {
    flash: { enabled: true, duration: 600, onEdit: false },
  },
})

flash: true is exactly flash: { enabled: true }.

Option Default Meaning
enabled false Off by default
duration 600 ms, covering rise and fall
onEdit false Flash the cell the user just finished editing

Off by default because a grid that is not live-updating should not flash when the developer calls updateRow() from a form save.

onEdit is off because the user knows what they typed — a flash is for changes arriving from somewhere else.

One duration for the whole flash, rather than separate fade and hold halves nobody has an opinion about.

Per column

const columns: ColumnDef<Tick>[] = [
  { field: 'symbol', header: 'Symbol' },
  { field: 'price', header: 'Price', display: { flash: 'up-down' } },
  { field: 'updatedAt', header: 'Updated', display: { flash: false } },
]
display.flash Behaviour
unset Inherit appearance.flash.enabled
true Flash in the neutral highlight colour
'up-down' Green when the value rose, red when it fell
false Never flash this column

'up-down' on a non-numeric column falls back to the neutral flash and warns once for that column.

The usual shape is flash: true grid-wide with flash: false on a "Last Updated" column, which changes on every update and says nothing by flashing.

It cannot false-positive

The trigger is a data event. Filtering, sorting, searching, paging and scrolling never emit it, so none of them can flash a cell that did not change.

The trigger is a real value change, not a re-render — so filtering or scrolling never lights a cell up, and there is no option needed to undo that.

Flashing on demand

api.flashCells([
  { rowId: 'row-1', columnId: 'price' },
  { rowId: 'row-9' }, // the whole row
])

A list of cells, not a cross product. Asking for A1 and B2 lights up exactly those two.

The argument is a list of individual cells, not a row set crossed with a column set — so A1 and B2 flash without lighting up A2 and B1, which is the scattered shape a live feed actually produces. Rows are named by id string here, as they are everywhere else in the API.

Cells that are not currently rendered are still registered, and flash if they scroll into view before the window expires.

Gotchas

  • update merges; it does not replace. Send only what changed.
  • remove takes ids, not rows. A Set works.
  • Check result.skipped on anything fed from outside your app — a drifted id is otherwise invisible.
  • applied ≠ skipped.length === 0.
  • Infinite scroll needs dataSource, not data, and InfiniteScrollModule is not in AllModules.
  • Infinite scroll and pagination are mutually exclusive. Registering both warns and disables one.
  • Flash is off by default, and a failed fetch leaves loaded rows on screen rather than blanking them.

Next: 11 · Events

toc.text: update merges, it does not replace
The result tells you what happened

chapters.title: Localization & State
chapters.blurb: Translating every string; saving and restoring a view
chapters.html:
Two features that tax every other one, so they are worth setting up early:

  • Localization — every string the grid renders, overridable.
  • Grid state — saved views: column layout, sort, filters, search, grouping, pagination, selection, scroll.

Neither needs a module.

Localization

Every string the grid renders has a key, and you override the ones you care about:

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  locale: {
    filterApply: 'Anwenden',
    filterClear: 'Löschen',
    filterOpContains: 'enthält',
  },
})

Partial by design. Anything you leave out stays English, so overriding three strings for tone is as legitimate as translating all 250.

Parameterised strings are functions

Not strings with placeholder tokens — which is what lets a translation reorder or pluralise them:

locale: {
  paginationPage: (page) => `Seite ${page}`,
  paginationRowCount: (from, to, total) => `${from}–${to} von ${total}`,
  groupCount: (count) => `${count} ${count === 1 ? 'Eintrag' : 'Einträge'}`,
}

A token-based string like 'Page {page} of {total}' cannot express a plural rule or a different word order. A function can.

Finding the keys

Keys are grouped by the surface they belong to, so autocomplete is useful:

Prefix Covers
filterOp* Filter operators — contains, between, before…
filter* The filter popover's own chrome
floatingFilter* The floating filter row
setFilter* The set filter's summary and list
pagination* The pagination bar
group* Group headings, counts, the chip bar, menu items

The full list with its English defaults is DEFAULT_LOCALE in the package source.

Catching what you missed

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  locale: myGermanLocale,
  localeStrict: true, // dev-only
})

Warns once, listing every key still rendering English. Opt-in rather than on by default, because a partial override is a legitimate choice rather than a mistake.

The grid's own label

accessibility: {
  gridLabel: 'Rechnungen', // overrides locale.gridLabel for this grid
}

accessibility.gridLabel predates locale and still wins for this one string — the narrow option beats the broad one.

Turning announcements down

accessibility: {
  announceFocus: true,      // default
  announceSort: true,       // default
  announceFilter: true,     // default
  announceSelection: true,  // default
  announceEdit: true,       // default
  announcePage: true,       // default
  announceRowsLoaded: true, // default — "200 of 12,480 rows loaded"
}

All on by default. See Accessibility.

Grid state

Everything the user arranged, in one serialisable object:

const saved = api.getState()
localStorage.setItem('myGrid', JSON.stringify(saved))
const report = api.setState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('myGrid')!))

Let the grid persist it for you

const grid = createGrid<Row>({
  modules: [AllModules],
  columns,
  data,
  state: {
    key: 'invoices-grid', // persist here, restore on mount
    debounce: 200,        // default
  },
})

That is the whole setup — no serialiser, no debounce, no version check to write.

debounce defaults to 200ms because scroll alone fires per frame, and an undebounced write would be a synchronous serialise on the scroll path.

What a state holds

Slice Contents
columns Width, order, visibility, pinning — and which column groups are folded
sort The sort model
filters The filter model
search The quick-filter text
grouping { model, expanded } — which columns are grouped and which sections are open
pagination { page, pageSize }
selection { ids }
rowDetail { expanded } — row ids whose detail panel is open
scroll { top, left }

A slice is absent only when the module that owns it is not registered.

Group expansion survives a reload, because a group is addressed by its key path — plain strings that JSON handles with no custom serialiser, and nothing that points at an internal row object.

Choosing what to persist

state: {
  key: 'invoices-grid',
  include: ['columns', 'sort', 'filters'], // not selection or scroll
}

Default is every slice the grid produces.

Restoring a subset

api.setState(saved, { only: ['columns'] }) // layout back, filters untouched

A restore tells you what happened

const report = api.setState(saved)

if (report.skipped.length > 0) {
  console.warn('partial restore', report.skipped)
}
Field Meaning
applied Slices that were restored
skipped { slice, reason, detail? } for each one that was not
reason Cause
'absent-module' The module that owns the slice is not registered
'not-in-state' The saved object has no such slice
'excluded' You passed only and this slice was not in it
'schema-mismatch' The saved state is from an incompatible version

It returns a report rather than void, which is what makes a partial restore visible — otherwise a saved view comes back "mostly" and nobody notices the filters are missing until a user does. expect(report.skipped).toEqual([]) is a test anyone can write.

initial vs key

state: {
  initial: savedFromMyServer, // restore this object once
}

initial is applied once, after the first data settle — not at construction. With an async dataSource there are no rows yet when the grid is built, so a restored selection would select nothing and a restored scroll offset would exceed a zero-height canvas.

Pipeline inputs — columns, sort, filters, search, page size — still apply immediately.

key and initial are independent: key persists to storage and restores from it, initial restores an object you supply. Use initial when the state comes from your own server rather than the browser.

Reacting to changes

events: {
  onStateChange: (state) => saveToServer(state),
}

Already debounced by state.debounce, so it is safe to persist directly from here. It fires whether or not state.key is set.

Functions do not serialise

A comparator or customFilter declared on the column is re-attached on restore, so a column with a custom sort keeps it.

One passed imperatively — to setSortModel() or setColumnFilter() — is dropped, with a development warning. If you want a custom comparator to survive a saved view, declare it on the column.

Gotchas

  • locale is partial. Untranslated keys stay English silently; localeStrict: true in development is how you find them.
  • Parameterised locale entries are functions, not templates with tokens.
  • accessibility.gridLabel beats locale.gridLabel.
  • state.initial applies after the first data settle, not at construction — so a selection restore works with an async source.
  • Check report.skipped. A half-restored view is otherwise invisible.
  • Declare comparators on the column, not imperatively, if they must survive a restore.
  • A saved rowDetail is filtered against the rows that came back — a saved view of a deleted row does not reopen a panel for it.
